Its free plan covers listing syndication, applications, TransUnion screening, rent collection and maintenance tracking, and more than 500,000 landlords use it. Paid tiers add state-specific leases, unlimited e-signatures and faster payouts and are billed annually. It is not designed for managers handling third-party properties, and accounting depth is thin next to DoorLoop.

Innago is free with no monthly fee, setup fee or unit limit, and it covers rent collection, screening, leases, maintenance and basic accounting with a mobile app. Support is consistently praised in reviews. The trade-offs are a narrower feature set, few third-party integrations and no equivalent to DoorLoop's workflow automation, so it fits landlords and small managers rather than growing management companies.

Hemlane takes a different approach: software plus optional human services. Its higher tiers add 24/7 repair coordination, tenant placement and eviction mediation, which suits remote or out-of-state owners who want DoorLoop-style tools without doing the work themselves. Pricing is per unit plus a platform fee and climbs quickly on the full-service tier, approaching traditional management costs, and it is a smaller vendor than DoorLoop.

faq.question: What is the best free alternative to DoorLoop?
faq.answer: TurboTenant and Innago both offer free plans covering listings, screening, leases, rent collection and maintenance. Innago has no unit limit, while TurboTenant reserves state-specific leases and unlimited e-signatures for annual paid tiers.

faq.question: How much does DoorLoop cost?
faq.answer: Starter is $69 per month on annual billing ($99 monthly) for up to 10 units, with additional units at $3 each. Pro is $149 per month and Premium $209 per month on annual terms, and portfolios over 300 units need a custom quote.

faq.question: Which DoorLoop alternative is best for professional property managers?
faq.answer: Buildium, from $62 per month, is the usual step up for third-party managers who need trust accounting and owner statements. Rentec Direct's PM edition, from $50 per month, is the lower-cost alternative.

faq.question: Is TenantCloud cheaper than DoorLoop?
faq.answer: Yes for small portfolios. TenantCloud's Starter plan is $15 per month on annual billing for up to 10 leases, versus DoorLoop's $69 for up to 10 units, though TenantCloud caps plans by lease count.

tenantcloud.intro:
TenantCloud is cloud property management software for landlords and small managers, with separate apps for landlords, tenants, owners and service providers. It covers online rent collection, screening, listing syndication to Apartments.com and Realtor.com, QuickBooks accounting, maintenance requests and e-signatures. Its pricing has changed. The free Starter plan that made it popular is gone; Starter is now $15 per month on annual billing, or $18 monthly, and it is capped at 10 leases. Growth allows 30 leases at about $29 per month, Pro allows 60 at $50, and Business is custom from $100, all with a 14-day trial. Those lease caps are the main reason landlords look elsewhere: a growing portfolio is forced up a tier even if it needs no new features. The lease builder, inspections and QuickBooks sync are also reserved for higher plans.

The good news is that this segment has plenty of options. Landlords who mainly want screening, leases and rent collection can get that free with no unit limit. Owners who care most about bookkeeping and tax time should choose an accounting-first tool. Flat-rate platforms remove the lease-count math entirely, and per-unit professional systems make sense once you manage for other owners.

picks.reason: TurboTenant is the most direct swap for landlords who used TenantCloud's old free tier. Its free plan includes listing syndication, applications, TransUnion screening, rent collection and maintenance tracking with no lease cap, and paid tiers add state-specific leases and unlimited e-signatures on annual billing. It is aimed at self-managing landlords, so professional managers handling other owners' properties will outgrow it.

Innago is free for landlords with no monthly fee, setup fee, contract or unit limit, which removes TenantCloud's lease-count problem entirely. It covers rent collection, screening, lease management, maintenance and accounting, with a mobile app and support that reviewers consistently rate highly. Integrations are limited and the feature set is lighter than paid platforms, so it fits landlords and small managers rather than larger companies.

RentRedi is the flat-rate choice: $29.95 per month, or $12 per month on annual billing, for unlimited units, tenants and team members. It includes ACH, card and cash rent payments at 90,000+ retail locations, TransUnion screening and maintenance requests with photo and video, and it is the official software for BiggerPockets members. Accounting is thinner than TenantCloud's QuickBooks-connected books.

Landlord Studio is the accounting-first alternative. Its free Go tier covers up to 3 units, and Pro is $12 per month plus $1 per additional unit, adding bank feeds, AI bookkeeping, more than 15 reports including Schedule E preparation and Xero integration, alongside listings, screening and rent collection. It is built for self-managing landlords and small investors, not for third-party managers or commercial assets.

Rentec Direct is the step up for landlords who are becoming professional managers. Starter is $25 per month for up to 10 properties, Pro and PM editions start at $50 per month with unlimited properties, and the PM edition adds trust accounting, owner portals and statements. Tenants get free ACH payments and support is US-based. The interface is older-looking and the mobile app is more limited than TenantCloud's.

DoorLoop is the fuller all-in-one for landlords who want more automation than TenantCloud offers, including an AI assistant, custom workflows, CAM charges for commercial units and listing syndication. Starter is $69 per month on annual billing for up to 10 units with $3 per extra unit, and Pro is $149. It costs considerably more than TenantCloud at the same portfolio size, and the AI features require the Pro plan.

faq.question: Is TenantCloud still free?
faq.answer: No. TenantCloud replaced its free plan with paid tiers. Starter is $15 per month on annual billing ($18 monthly) for up to 10 leases, with a 14-day trial.

faq.question: What is the best free alternative to TenantCloud?
faq.answer: Innago is free with no unit limit, and TurboTenant's free plan covers listings, screening, applications and rent collection. Landlord Studio's free tier covers up to 3 units with an accounting focus.

faq.question: Which TenantCloud alternative has no lease or unit caps?
faq.answer: RentRedi charges a flat $29.95 per month, or $12 per month on annual billing, for unlimited units, and Innago is free with no limits.

faq.question: What should a landlord choose when moving into managing properties for others?
faq.answer: Rentec Direct's PM edition, from $50 per month, adds trust accounting and owner statements, and Buildium from $62 per month is the common next step for full third-party management.

propertyshark.intro:
PropertyShark is a property research and prospecting database owned by Yardi, priced from $60 per month with a free trial. It suits individual brokers, investors and appraisers who need owner lookup, comparable sales, permits, zoning and foreclosure tracking without a CoStar contract. The reasons people look elsewhere follow from its cons: coverage is uneven outside New York City and a few major metros, the dataset is smaller than CoStar's, the interface feels dated, and there are no transaction or property management features. Teams that prospect nationally, or that need verified owner phone numbers and emails rather than names and mailing addresses, tend to outgrow it fastest.

Start by naming the job PropertyShark does for you. If it is finding true owners behind LLCs and building call lists, a dedicated ownership-intelligence tool covers that better and nationally. If it is parcel maps and zoning, a map-first platform will be cleaner. If you need bulk data feeding a model or CRM, a licensed data provider with an API is the right shape, even if it costs more. And if you actually need lease comps and market analytics across property types, the honest answer is a CoStar subscription, which PropertyShark was never meant to replace.

picks.reason: Reonomy, now part of Altus Group, is the closest like-for-like upgrade for prospecting: national coverage, AI-connected ownership records that surface the people behind LLCs and trusts, and debt maturity data for finding motivated sellers. A free trial lets you compare coverage in your market first. Pricing is not published, and like PropertyShark its data is strongest in major metros with limited lease detail.

PropTracer is built for one job: verified owner contact details for commercial and residential parcels, with map-based search, bulk CSV export and dynamic lists that refresh as records change. Choose it if PropertyShark's owner lookup gets you a name but not a working phone number. Pricing is quote-based, and accuracy can lag on very recently transferred properties.

Plotzy covers 150M+ parcels across 3,200+ counties, which fills PropertyShark's gaps outside New York and the major metros, and adds two-level zoning filters plus owner contact lookup for outreach. It costs more, from $180 a month, and is still labeled beta, so a single-market user who only needs occasional owner lookups will find PropertyShark cheaper.

Land id is the low-cost option, with a free plan and paid plans from $9.99 per month, covering parcel lines, ownership and comparable sales in all 50 states with branded interactive maps. It fits land, rural and suburban work far better than dense urban commercial, so NYC-focused PropertyShark users will find it thin for their core market.

LightBox Vision, formerly LandVision, is a nationwide map-first platform with parcel boundaries, building footprints, ownership and zoning data, plus in-platform report ordering. It suits site selection and ownership research teams that want consistent coverage rather than PropertyShark's metro-by-metro depth. It is enterprise-oriented with contact-for-pricing plans, so budget for a sales process.

ATTOM is the choice when you need data as a feed rather than a search screen: deeds, mortgages, foreclosures, permits and AVMs on more than 160 million US properties, delivered by API, bulk files or Snowflake and Databricks shares. It is right for brokerages and investors building their own tooling. Pricing is negotiated per license and it requires technical integration to be useful.

CoStar is the step up rather than sideways: the largest US commercial database, with lease comps, sales transactions and submarket analytics at a depth PropertyShark does not attempt. Choose it when you have outgrown owner lookup and need market intelligence across property types. The cost is real: premium pricing, annual contracts and a steep learning curve that smaller firms often cannot justify.

faq.question: Is PropertyShark good outside New York City?
faq.answer: PropertyShark covers major US metros, but its data is deepest in New York City and coverage varies noticeably by market. Users outside its core markets often pair it with, or replace it with, a nationwide platform such as Reonomy or LightBox Vision.

faq.question: What is the cheapest alternative to PropertyShark?
faq.answer: Land id offers a free plan and paid plans from $9.99 per month for parcel, ownership and comparable sales data across all 50 states, though it is strongest for land and rural property rather than urban commercial buildings.

faq.question: Which PropertyShark alternative is best for contacting property owners?
faq.answer: PropTracer and Reonomy both specialize in identifying true owners behind LLCs. PropTracer focuses on verified phone numbers, emails and mailing addresses with bulk export for CRMs and direct mail, while Reonomy adds debt maturity and transaction history to help prioritize who to call.

faq.question: Is PropertyShark cheaper than CoStar?
faq.answer: Yes. PropertyShark publishes a starting price of $60 per month with a free trial, while CoStar is enterprise-priced on annual contracts. The trade-off is a smaller dataset with no transaction or property management features.

matterport.intro:
Matterport is the default platform for 3D digital twins in real estate, used for listing tours, floor plans, facilities documentation and construction coordination. It has a free tier, smartphone capture, paid plans from $11.49 per month for 5 active spaces up to $277.99 for 100, and integrations with LoopNet, Zillow, VTS and Autodesk. People look for alternatives for a few consistent reasons. Per-space pricing grows quickly across a large portfolio, the best results still require a Matterport camera costing $3,000 or more, the models are cloud-dependent and need good bandwidth, and CoStar Group's acquisition of Matterport, completed in early 2025, has some users rethinking vendor concentration.

Which Matterport feature you rely on decides the replacement. If it is measured floor plans and reports, a capture system built for accuracy will beat it. If it is simple 360 tours for listings, a lower-cost tour builder that works with any 360 camera is enough. If it is jobsite documentation, construction-specific capture tools do that job better. And if it is polished listing media in general, a per-image editing service may cost less than a subscription you rarely use.

picks.reason: iGUIDE is the closest replacement for the measurement side of Matterport: one capture with its PLANIX camera produces a 3D tour, ANSI-compliant floor plans with a stated 0.5 percent uncertainty, and exports to DWG, CAD and Revit. Pricing is per project with no subscription, and users own their data. The catch is buying the proprietary camera at $3,499 CAD or hiring an iGUIDE Pro.

CloudPano is the budget route for listing tours: upload 360 photos from any camera, link scenes with hotspots, add dollhouse floor plans, and publish or embed, from $22.50 per month billed annually with a free tier. It suits agents and property managers who need tours, not digital twins. The entry plan caps you at 3 published projects and team features sit on the pricier Commercial tier.

RICOH360 Tours pairs a free tier and a $39 per month Pro plan, billed annually, with unlimited tours, AI image enhancement, virtual staging and a floor plan generator. It is a good fit if you already shoot with a THETA camera. Floor plans cost $20 each beyond the first order and extra team seats are paid add-ons, so it is best for small teams.

BoxBrownie is a different approach: instead of software, you order per-image edits such as virtual staging, day-to-dusk, floor plan redraws, 3D renders and 360 image editing, priced from 2 euros per image with no subscription. Choose it when your Matterport plan is really paying for listing media. Human editors mean a 24 to 48 hour turnaround rather than an instant model.

OpenSpace replaces Matterport specifically for construction progress capture: 360 cameras, phones or drones walk the site and imagery is auto-mapped to floor plans and BIM models with timestamps, plus integrations with Procore and Autodesk. It fits general contractors and owners tracking builds, not marketing. Pricing is quote-based and it needs a consistent capture routine to pay off.

faq.question: Is Matterport still an independent company?
faq.answer: No. CoStar Group completed its acquisition of Matterport on February 28, 2025, in a deal valued at about $1.6 billion, and Matterport now operates as part of CoStar Group.

faq.question: What is the cheapest alternative to Matterport for virtual tours?
faq.answer: RICOH360 Tours and CloudPano both offer free tiers, with paid plans at $39 and $22.50 per month respectively when billed annually. Both build tours from 360 photos rather than a dedicated Matterport camera.

faq.question: Do I need a special camera to replace Matterport?
faq.answer: Not always. CloudPano and RICOH360 Tours accept 360 photos from consumer cameras, and Matterport itself supports smartphone capture. iGUIDE, by contrast, requires its PLANIX camera or a hired iGUIDE Pro because its floor plans depend on measured scans.

faq.question: Which Matterport alternative produces accurate floor plans?
faq.answer: iGUIDE produces ANSI/RMS-compliant floor plans with a stated measurement uncertainty of 0.5 percent and exports to DWG, CAD and Revit formats, which makes it the usual pick for appraisal, insurance and construction workflows.

visuallease.intro:
Visual Lease is an enterprise lease administration and lease accounting platform covering the full lease lifecycle plus ASC 842, IFRS 16 and GASB 87 compliance for both real estate and equipment leases. CoStar Group acquired it in November 2024 and is aligning it with its Real Estate Manager business. It fits large corporate occupiers with finance, legal, procurement and real estate teams sharing one lease record. The reasons people look elsewhere are consistent: enterprise-only pricing on annual contracts, implementations that run long for complex global portfolios, screens that still feel dated while the interface is modernized, and uncertainty about pricing and roadmap under new ownership.

Decide which half of Visual Lease you actually use. Finance teams that mostly need journal entries, disclosures and audit-ready compliance can move to an accounting-first tool that is simpler and often faster to implement. Real estate teams that live in critical dates, renewals and transactions may be better served by a tenant-side lease management platform. If leases are one piece of a larger facilities and portfolio problem, an IWMS with a lease accounting module consolidates vendors. Smaller portfolios that want people alongside software have service-led options too.

picks.reason: FinQuery, formerly LeaseQuery, is the most direct swap for the accounting side: ASC 842, IFRS 16 and GASB 87 compliance with automated journal entries and disclosure reporting, sold to organizations from small businesses to large enterprises. It also handles prepaids and accruals. Pricing is quote-based, and operational lease management is thinner than Visual Lease, so real estate teams may still need a separate tool.

Lease Harbor covers both lease administration and lease accounting in one system, with FASB, IFRS and GASB compliance, configurable reporting, ERP integrations and turn-key implementations advertised in days. Its 25-plus years and 1,800-plus clients make it the closest independent equivalent for mid-size to Fortune 100 portfolios. There is no published pricing and no free trial.

Occupier is built for tenants and tenant-rep brokers rather than accountants: lease abstraction, critical dates, approval workflows and transaction management with ASC 842 compliance included, and a free trial. It fits corporate real estate teams managing office, retail or industrial leases. It is a smaller company, unsuitable for landlord operations, and pricing is not published.

Quarem pairs lease management software with a dedicated in-house services team that abstracts leases, tracks critical dates and payments, and knows your portfolio. Choose it if implementation effort and internal staffing are what make Visual Lease hard. The service-led model is less scalable and less technically ambitious than pure SaaS, and pricing is set per engagement.

Nakisa offers lease accounting for all three major standards inside a broader IWMS that also covers portfolio management, capital projects and facility management, with ties to HR and finance data. It suits enterprises that want one vendor for real estate operations and lease compliance. Full IWMS deployment is complex, and it has less US CRE recognition than the specialists.

Accruent, owned by Fortive, bundles lease administration and ASC 842 and IFRS 16 accounting into a facilities and asset management suite used across healthcare, retail, education and government. It makes sense when leases are one of several building problems you need to manage. Expect enterprise pricing, a heavy implementation and some dated modules from its acquisition history.

faq.question: Who owns Visual Lease?
faq.answer: CoStar Group. It announced the acquisition in October 2024 and closed it on November 1, 2024, adding Visual Lease to its CoStar Real Estate Manager business line.

faq.question: What is the best alternative to Visual Lease for ASC 842 compliance only?
faq.answer: FinQuery, formerly LeaseQuery, is the most focused option, automating journal entries, disclosures and compliance for ASC 842, IFRS 16 and GASB 87 without a full operational lease management layer.

faq.question: Is there a Visual Lease alternative with a free trial?
faq.answer: Occupier offers a free trial of its tenant-focused lease management and ASC 842 platform. Visual Lease, FinQuery, Lease Harbor and Nakisa are all quote-based with no published free trial.

faq.question: Can an IWMS replace Visual Lease?
faq.answer: For enterprises that also manage space, facilities and capital projects, yes: Nakisa, Accruent, Planon and IBM TRIRIGA all include lease accounting modules. Companies that only need lease administration and accounting usually find a dedicated tool simpler and quicker to implement.

archibus.intro:
Archibus is a long-established Integrated Workplace Management System, now sold as part of Eptura's worktech portfolio alongside the former iOFFICE and SpaceIQ products. It covers space planning, asset and facility management, preventive maintenance, visitor management and employee experience, with Autodesk integration and FedRAMP authorization for government clients. It fits large enterprises and public agencies with complex portfolios. The reasons people look elsewhere follow from its scope: quote-based enterprise pricing, a platform that is far more than most mid-size organizations need, and product-line confusion after the Eptura rebrand.

The right replacement depends on which Archibus modules carry your workload. If you need the whole IWMS, the direct competitors are other enterprise suites, and switching is a multi-year project. If maintenance and work orders are the core, a modern CMMS is cheaper and faster to deploy. If space planning and test-fitting for corporate real estate is the job, a focused workplace design tool covers it without the rest of the suite. Be honest about how many modules you actually run before you buy another all-in-one system.

picks.reason: Planon is the most direct like-for-like IWMS: portfolio, space and workplace management, facilities and maintenance, lease accounting, sustainability and field services, recognized by Verdantix, Gartner and IDC. It suits global enterprises and universities that want a single platform from an independent vendor. It is EMEA-centric with a smaller US footprint, and implementation needs specialized consulting.

IBM TRIRIGA, now packaged as IBM Maximo Real Estate and Facilities, matches Archibus module for module and adds Maximo's broader asset management. It is the pick for Fortune 500 occupiers already standardized on IBM. Costs are IBM-scale, implementations usually involve IBM consultants, and the fold into Maximo Application Suite adds transition risk.

Accruent offers IWMS capabilities across space, lease administration and accounting, capital planning, maintenance and IoT monitoring, with strong verticals in healthcare, retail, education and government. Choose it over Archibus if lease compliance or multi-industry support matters more than workplace experience features. The portfolio sprawls from acquisitions and some modules feel dated.

Tango covers the property lifecycle from site selection to sustainability, with lease management, space utilization, projects, maintenance and energy tracking, and unusually strong retail features such as store performance prediction. It fits corporate and retail occupiers with many locations. It offers little for investment or brokerage use, and enterprise pricing applies.

Facilio is the focused alternative if Archibus is mostly running your work orders: an AI-powered CMMS with preventive maintenance, inspections, vendor management, energy monitoring and a mobile app for field teams, across commercial portfolios. It drops the space and workplace modules, so it suits operations teams rather than corporate real estate planners. Pricing is quote-based with no free trial.

Saltmine replaces the space planning slice of Archibus for corporate real estate teams: space programming, test fits, visualization and project delivery with unlimited users, built by architects. It is the choice when planning speed matters more than facilities operations. It is not an IWMS, implementation runs 4 to 8 weeks, and results depend on clean data inputs.

faq.question: Is Archibus the same as Eptura?
faq.answer: Archibus is one product within Eptura, the company formed by combining iOFFICE and SpaceIQ. Eptura sells Archibus alongside its other workplace and asset management tools.

faq.question: What is the closest alternative to Archibus for a full IWMS?
faq.answer: Planon, IBM TRIRIGA (now IBM Maximo Real Estate and Facilities) and Accruent are the closest full-suite competitors, covering space, facilities, maintenance, leases and sustainability for enterprise portfolios.

faq.question: Is there a cheaper alternative to Archibus for maintenance management?
faq.answer: Facilio and other CMMS platforms cover work orders, preventive maintenance, inspections and vendor management without the full IWMS footprint. Facilio's pricing is quote-based, so cost still needs to be confirmed against your portfolio size.

faq.question: Does Archibus publish pricing?
faq.answer: No. Archibus pricing is quote-based through Eptura and depends on modules and portfolio size, which is also true of Planon, IBM TRIRIGA, Accruent, Tango, Facilio and Saltmine.

cherre.intro:
Cherre is a data management layer for institutional real estate: it ingests internal system data and 150-plus external sources, normalizes everything into a Universal Data Model, and delivers clean data to warehouses, BI tools and its Agent STUDIO for AI workflows. It connects to Yardi, MRI, CoStar, ARGUS, Snowflake and Databricks. It fits asset and investment managers with large, multi-system portfolios. The reasons people look elsewhere are structural: enterprise-only annual pricing, a payoff that depends on having data engineering capacity in-house, implementations that get complex with messy sources, and the fact that Cherre is the pipe rather than the data, so you still pay each underlying provider.

Separate the two things Cherre does. If the problem is stitching your own operating and accounting systems into one reporting view, a CRE-specific analytics platform with prebuilt connectors can do that with less engineering. If the problem is acquiring external property, ownership, debt or transaction data, go directly to the vendors that deliver via API or cloud shares and load it yourself. Most mid-size firms do not need a universal data model; they need two or three good feeds and a warehouse.

picks.reason: NavigatorCRE is the most direct alternative for internal data centralization: it connects accounting, leasing, collections, debt, construction and work-order systems into one cloud analytics layer with NAVI AI, across all asset classes. It suits asset managers and developers who want dashboards faster than a data engineering project. It is smaller than Cherre or the major platforms and pricing is quote-based.

ATTOM delivers property characteristics, deeds, mortgages, foreclosures, permits, AVMs and risk models on more than 160 million US properties by API, bulk file, Snowflake and Databricks shares, plus MCP support for AI tools. Choose it when you want raw feeds into your own warehouse rather than a managed data model. It is negotiated per license and needs technical integration.

Reonomy, an Altus Group business, is the right swap if what you wanted from Cherre was property intelligence rather than plumbing: AI-connected ownership, debt maturity and transaction records searchable in a web app, with a free trial. It suits investors and brokers doing sourcing and research. Data quality varies by market, lease data is thin, and pricing is not published.

CRED iQ focuses on the securitized debt slice: CMBS, SASB, CRE CLO and agency multifamily loans covering roughly $2.3 trillion, with maturity dates, special servicing status, borrower contacts and property operating statements, via web app, API or bulk feed. It fits lenders and distressed investors. Coverage outside securitized debt is limited and pricing is quote-based.

MSCI Real Capital Analytics is the institutional choice for transaction data and benchmarking: global sales records, investor and lender profiles and 80-plus performance indexes across 170-plus countries, plus climate risk analytics. Fund managers use it for attribution and screening rather than operations. It is very expensive, institutional-only, backward-looking by design, and has a steep learning curve.

CoStar is the single-vendor alternative: the largest US commercial database with building, ownership, lease comp, sales and submarket analytics in one subscription, with no integration project required. It suits teams that need market intelligence rather than a unified data platform. The trade-offs are premium annual contracts, a steep learning curve, and buying one vendor's dataset rather than integrating many.

faq.question: Is Cherre a data provider or a data platform?
faq.answer: Cherre is primarily a data integration and management platform. It connects and normalizes data from a client's internal systems and 150-plus external partners into a Universal Data Model, so clients generally still license underlying datasets from the providers themselves.

faq.question: What is the cheapest alternative to Cherre?
faq.answer: None of the direct alternatives publish pricing. Reonomy offers a free trial for property intelligence, and NavigatorCRE positions itself as a low-IT-lift way to centralize CRE data, but both are quote-based like Cherre.

faq.question: Which Cherre alternative is best for CRE debt data?
faq.answer: CRED iQ specializes in securitized commercial real estate debt, covering CMBS, SASB, CRE CLO and agency multifamily loans with maturity, servicing and borrower data delivered by web app, API or bulk feed.

faq.question: Can I replace Cherre with Snowflake or Databricks?
faq.answer: Partly. Both are data warehouses that Cherre itself delivers into. Vendors such as ATTOM provide direct Snowflake and Databricks data shares, so a team with its own data engineers can load feeds directly and skip the managed data model.

airdna.intro:
AirDNA is the most widely used short-term rental analytics platform, tracking Airbnb and Vrbo listings worldwide with market-level occupancy, daily rate and revenue data, a Rentalizer that estimates income for any address, and comp sets for benchmarking. It has a free tier, a Research plan at $34 per month billed annually or $125 monthly, a Host plan at $50 per month annually or $150 monthly, and a custom-priced Property Manager plan. It fits investors screening markets and hosts pricing against competitors. People look for alternatives because monthly billing costs three to four times the annual rate, accuracy drops in smaller and emerging markets, the manager tier has no published price, and Rentalizer estimates are only a starting point for underwriting.

Match the alternative to the decision you are making. If you are screening a purchase, a free address-level calculator may be all you need before you pay for anything. If you are comparing short-term against long-term rental returns, an investment analytics tool that covers both is more useful than deeper STR data alone. If you manage a portfolio, benchmarking built on verified reservation data from property management systems is more reliable than scraped calendars. And if the goal is pricing and channel performance, that lives in your property management software.

picks.reason: Mashvisor is the closest replacement for investors: short-term and long-term rental estimates side by side with cap rates and cash-on-cash returns, a Market Finder and Property Finder across the US, AI dynamic pricing for hosts, and a data API. It publishes tiered plan prices. Accuracy thins in small and rural markets, API access sits on the expensive plans, and coverage is US-only.

Rabbu is the free option: an Airbnb calculator with occupancy, ADR, RevPAN and seasonalized monthly revenue for any US address, market pages with an ROI Score, and a Chrome extension that overlays projections on listings. It is enough for first-pass screening before paying for AirDNA. It is STR-only, US-only, and its projections are listing-based estimates that need validation.

Key Data builds its benchmarks from verified reservation data via 80-plus property management system integrations, not scraped listing calendars, and layers in hotel comps and OTA market coverage. Choose it if you run a portfolio and need trustworthy pacing and occupancy comparisons. It is quote-based, sales-led, and aimed at managers and destination organizations rather than individual buyers.

Rentometer answers the long-term rental side that AirDNA ignores: hyperlocal rent estimates, comparable rentals, batch processing across a portfolio, branded reports and an API. It fits investors deciding whether a property should be a traditional rental at all. Free access is very limited, plans are contact-for-pricing, and it does not cover short-term rental performance.

Guesty is a different approach: a short-term rental property management platform with dynamic pricing, revenue management, a 60-plus channel manager, payments and trust accounting, starting at $9 per month for 1 to 3 listings. Choose it if your AirDNA use is really about pricing your own listings. Pro and Enterprise tiers are quote-based and the module breadth brings a learning curve.

Hostaway suits professional managers who want pricing and revenue tools inside a full PMS: a channel manager across 100-plus OTAs, unified messaging, task automation and an AI CoHost for guest communication. It replaces the operational half of AirDNA's Property Manager plan rather than its market research. Pricing is quote-based by listing count, and single-listing hosts are routed to a separate path.

faq.question: Is there a free alternative to AirDNA?
faq.answer: Rabbu offers a free Airbnb revenue calculator and market data pages for US addresses, and AirDNA's own free tier includes limited Rentalizer and Market Insights access.

faq.question: How much does AirDNA cost?
faq.answer: AirDNA's Research plan is $34 per month billed annually or $125 month to month, the Host plan is $50 per month annually or $150 monthly, and the Property Manager plan is custom priced.

faq.question: Which AirDNA alternative compares short-term and long-term rental returns?
faq.answer: Mashvisor provides both Airbnb and traditional rental estimates with cap rate and cash-on-cash calculations for the same property, while Rentometer covers long-term rent comps only.

faq.question: Is AirDNA data accurate?
faq.answer: AirDNA compiles data from millions of Airbnb and Vrbo listings and is widely used, but accuracy can vary in smaller or emerging markets. Key Data uses verified reservation data from property management system integrations, which is more reliable for benchmarking a managed portfolio.

zoneomics.intro:
Zoneomics is the zoning reference most CRE teams reach for first. It digitizes zoning and land use codes from thousands of cities into the largest nationwide zoning dataset, layers AI analysis on top, sells reports from $25 and certified zoning letters for closings, and exposes everything through an API. The reasons people look elsewhere are consistent: coverage is uneven, since not every city is fully digitized, the free search shows little without buying a report, per-report and per-letter costs add up for teams that check zoning every day, and it stops at the answer. Zoneomics tells you what a parcel allows; it does not help you find the next twenty parcels or reach their owners.

So start with the job. If zoning is the deliverable, you need a certified letter or a bulk code feed, the alternatives are thin and Zoneomics usually stays. If zoning is a filter on the way to a site or a prospect list, a parcel search platform with zoning attached to every record replaces it for most daily work, and a data vendor covers the pipeline case. Most land and development teams end up with one sourcing tool and Zoneomics on standby for confirmation.

picks.reason: The most direct replacement for daily zoning research: every one of Plotzy's 150M+ parcels carries a two-level zoning designation, so you filter a corridor, county or polygon by permitted use, lot size and owner type in one pass, then pull owner contacts and export the list. A Zoning AI chat covers the code questions Zoneomics reports answer. Flat pricing from $180 a month replaces per-report spend, with a 7-day trial and no card. It does not issue certified zoning letters, it is still labeled beta, and sub-level zoning depth varies by municipality.

Gridics converts ordinances into parcel-level development-allowance data with a patented rules engine, and its PropZone product wraps that in property research and site selection tools with 3D development capacity. Pick it when you need buildable-envelope math, not just the zoning label. Depth depends on which municipalities have been onboarded, pricing is quote-based, and feasibility reports carry a services component.

Regrid sells standardized zoning as an enrichment on complete US parcel data, delivered by API, tiles or bulk files. Choose it when you have GIS analysts or engineers and want zoning inside your own tools rather than a website. It is a data product, not an analysis application, and zoning is a paid add-on with no published pricing.

LightBox Vision, the rebranded LandVision, puts zoning layers, parcel boundaries, ownership and in-platform report ordering in one enterprise mapping tool backed by LightBox datasets. Choose it for multi-seat teams already buying from LightBox. Pricing is annual and on quote, and the feature set is heavier than most brokers need.

Archistar reads zoning rules, overlays and constraints and then generates code-compliant 3D massing options, so it answers what can be built rather than what the zoning says. Choose it for early feasibility on a shortlisted site. Planning-data depth is strongest in Australia and coverage varies elsewhere; pricing is not published.

TestFit is the feasibility step after zoning: map the parcel, generate building configurations and see the financial takeoffs in hours. Choose it when the zoning answer is already known and the question is whether the deal pencils. It is not a zoning lookup and needs a sales conversation for pricing.

faq.question: Is there a free alternative to Zoneomics?
faq.answer: Zoneomics itself offers a free basic zoning search. Among alternatives, Plotzy provides a 7-day free trial with no credit card, and most other zoning and parcel platforms are paid or quote-based.

faq.question: Which Zoneomics alternative also provides owner contacts?
faq.answer: Plotzy combines zoning filters with owner contact lookup, folders and CSV export, so a zoning search becomes a prospect list. LightBox Vision includes ownership data as well; Regrid provides ownership as a data enrichment.

faq.question: Who else provides certified zoning letters?
faq.answer: Certified zoning verification letters remain a Zoneomics strength. Gridics offers expert-prepared zoning feasibility reports; the parcel search platforms in this list do not issue certified letters.

faq.question: How does Plotzy compare to Zoneomics on coverage?
faq.answer: Plotzy covers 150M+ parcels across 3,200+ counties with a two-level zoning designation on every parcel; Zoneomics has the largest digitized code coverage but not every city is fully digitized. Check your target markets on both before committing.

landvision.intro:
LandVision, now sold as LightBox Vision, is the enterprise mapping platform from LightBox: parcel boundaries, building footprints, ownership, zoning layers and report ordering on one map, tied together by the LightBox ID that links records across the wider LightBox data ecosystem. It is a serious tool for large teams. The reasons people shop around are equally serious: pricing is annual and on quote, the rebrand created confusion about what is included, the feature set is heavier than a broker or small land team needs, and the enterprise sales process is slow when you want to start searching this week.

Decide which slice you use. If it is finding parcels and owners for prospecting, a modern parcel search tool with published pricing does the job at a fraction of the cost. If it is ownership and debt intelligence on existing commercial buildings, a property intelligence platform fits better. If it is the underlying data for your own GIS, buy the data directly. Few teams need all of LightBox Vision, which is why most alternatives below are narrower and cheaper.

picks.reason: For brokers and land teams the closest like-for-like replacement: nationwide parcel search across 150M+ parcels with two-level zoning on every record, owner contact lookup, folders and CSV export, at published month-to-month pricing of $180 to $300 and a 7-day trial with no credit card. You trade the LightBox ecosystem and environmental reports for speed and transparency. It is still labeled beta and integrations sit on the custom Scale plan.

Reonomy, an Altus Group business, is the pick when the parcels you care about have buildings on them: ownership unmasking through LLCs, debt maturity, transaction history and 200+ filters for investment sales prospecting. It is thinner on land and zoning, pricing is not published, and it is a research tool rather than a map-first workflow.

Regrid is the data layer without the application: 100% US parcel coverage with boundaries, building footprints, zoning and daily ownership updates, delivered by API, tiles or bulk files. Choose it when a GIS analyst or engineer will pipe parcels into your own stack. Pricing is quote-based and there is no research interface to speak of.

PropertyShark gives owner lookup, list building and foreclosure tracking from $60 a month with a free trial, which makes it the budget replacement for occasional ownership research. Coverage is strongest in New York City and major metros, and it lacks the zoning and mapping depth of LightBox Vision.

LandGlide is the mobile parcel viewer: tap a parcel in the field and see boundaries, owner and basic attributes on a phone. Choose it as a cheap field companion rather than a desk research platform. It has no prospecting workflow, contact intelligence or zoning analysis.

CoStar is the everything option: property, ownership, comps, analytics and marketplaces in one enterprise contract. Choose it when you need lease and sales comps alongside parcel research and the budget supports it. It is the most expensive path and overkill if parcel and owner lookup is the actual need.

faq.question: Is LandVision the same as LightBox Vision?
faq.answer: Yes. LandVision was rebranded as LightBox Vision after Digital Map Products became part of LightBox. The product remains a nationwide parcel mapping and property research platform.

faq.question: What is the cheapest LandVision alternative?
faq.answer: PropertyShark starts at $60 a month and LandGlide is a low-cost mobile parcel viewer. For a full prospecting workflow with zoning and owner contacts, Plotzy starts at $180 a month with a 7-day free trial.

faq.question: Which alternative is best for land and development sites?
faq.answer: Plotzy is built for land acquisition teams and developers, with two-level zoning on every parcel and sub-level zoning filters. CityBldr and TestFit are stronger once you need buildable-unit or feasibility math on a shortlisted site.

faq.question: Do these alternatives require an annual contract?
faq.answer: Plotzy and PropertyShark are month to month. Reonomy offers monthly and annual billing. LightBox Vision, Regrid and CoStar are typically sold on annual or enterprise terms.

comparisons.verdict:
Yardi and AppFolio both aim to run your entire property operation, but they come at it from opposite directions. Yardi is the 40-year incumbent with the broadest single-stack platform in the industry: Voyager for enterprise portfolios, Breeze (from $1/unit/month) for smaller operators, plus investment management, energy, and procurement suites that cover multifamily, commercial, affordable housing, senior living, and more across 80+ countries. AppFolio is the modern challenger: a cloud-only, AI-native platform built around agentic AI and its Realm-X workflow engine, serving residential managers from roughly 50 units up to 14,000+.

Yardi wins on breadth and property-type coverage. If you run commercial assets, affordable housing, or need fund accounting and an investor portal in the same stack, AppFolio simply does not go that deep. Yardi's trade-offs are real, though: Voyager has a steep learning curve, implementations can take months, and some modules feel dated. AppFolio wins on user experience and automation, with AI built into the core rather than bolted on, at the cost of quote-based pricing and a change-management lift for traditional teams.

Bottom line: diverse or institutional portfolios that need commercial and investment management pick Yardi; growing residential managers who value modern UX and AI automation pick AppFolio; very small landlords should compare Yardi Breeze against both.
comparisons.one_liner: Yardi wins on breadth across every property type; AppFolio wins on modern AI-native UX for growing residential managers.

faq.question: Is Yardi cheaper than AppFolio?
faq.answer: It depends on your size. Yardi Breeze publishes pricing from $1/unit/month ($2 for Breeze Premier), which is a genuinely affordable entry point, while Yardi Voyager and AppFolio are both quote-based, so you will need sales conversations to compare enterprise costs. AppFolio is generally positioned as premium pricing for its AI capabilities.

faq.question: Can AppFolio handle commercial properties like Yardi does?
faq.answer: AppFolio lists commercial among its supported property types, but its platform is built primarily for residential property managers. Yardi is the stronger choice for commercial portfolios, with dedicated commercial leasing tools, plus coverage for affordable housing, senior living, and coworking that AppFolio does not match.

faq.question: Which is easier to implement, Yardi or AppFolio?
faq.answer: AppFolio, generally. Yardi Voyager implementations are known to take months and the platform can be complex to configure, while AppFolio is a single cloud platform with a unified interface. That said, AppFolio's AI-native approach still requires training and change management for teams used to traditional software.

comparisons.verdict:
This is the classic enterprise real estate software matchup, and the honest answer is that philosophy matters more than features. Both platforms cover commercial and residential management, full accounting, and investment management for mid-market and enterprise portfolios. Yardi (founded 1984, self-funded, 9,000+ employees) is the closed single-stack approach: everything from property management to energy to procurement lives in one ecosystem. MRI (founded 1971, 50,000+ clients) is the open-platform approach, built to connect with 200+ integration partners so you can assemble best-of-breed tools around its core.

Yardi wins if you want one vendor for everything and a cheap on-ramp: Breeze starts at a published $1/unit/month, something MRI has no answer to, and the Voyager ecosystem is arguably the most comprehensive in real estate. The catch is lock-in; migrating off Yardi is notoriously difficult. MRI wins on flexibility, facilities management (MRI Angus is a standout), and AI-powered lease abstraction for commercial portfolios. Its weakness is product sprawl from acquisitions, which can mean inconsistent user experiences. Both have steep learning curves and lengthy implementations.

Bottom line: organizations that want a single accountable vendor and all-in-one depth pick Yardi; commercial-heavy portfolios that value integration freedom and strong facilities management pick MRI.
comparisons.one_liner: Yardi is the all-in-one closed ecosystem; MRI is the open platform with 200+ integrations. Pick by philosophy, not feature lists.

faq.question: Is MRI Software cheaper than Yardi?
faq.answer: Neither publishes enterprise pricing; both Voyager and MRI are quote-based, so costs depend on your portfolio and modules. Yardi does have a published low-cost entry point in Breeze (from $1/unit/month) for smaller portfolios, which MRI does not offer. For enterprise deals, get quotes from both.

faq.question: Which is better for commercial real estate, Yardi or MRI?
faq.answer: Both are credible for commercial. MRI has particularly deep commercial roots, with full-stack commercial management, AI lease abstraction via Lease Intelligence, and the Angus facilities platform. Yardi counters with COMMERCIALCafe and broader coverage of specialized types like coworking and senior living. Commercial-only shops often lean MRI; mixed portfolios often lean Yardi.

faq.question: Can I use third-party tools with Yardi and MRI?
faq.answer: MRI is explicitly built as an open platform with 200+ integration partners, including VTS and ARGUS, so best-of-breed stacks are a core selling point. Yardi favors its own ecosystem, and deep integration plus data lock-in makes leaving or mixing in outside tools harder. If integration flexibility matters, MRI has the edge.

comparisons.verdict:
Yardi and RealPage are both enterprise heavyweights, but they are not really solving the same problem. Yardi is a general-purpose real estate platform: property management, accounting, and investment management across multifamily, commercial, affordable, senior living, and coworking, with Breeze (from $1/unit/month) giving smaller operators a way in. RealPage is a multifamily specialist: its OneSite platform, Knock CRM, DemandX demand forecasting, and industry-leading revenue management are all purpose-built for apartment operators, and it does not seriously compete outside rental housing.

RealPage wins on multifamily depth. Its AI-driven revenue management, market analytics footprint, and Lumina AI workforce give large apartment operators optimization tools Yardi does not match, and the two even integrate, so some operators run RealPage tools on top of Yardi accounting. The caveats: RealPage is enterprise-priced with no small-portfolio option, has a steep learning curve, and its revenue management pricing algorithms have drawn DOJ antitrust scrutiny, which buyers should factor into diligence. Yardi wins on breadth, accounting depth, investment management, and having options at every portfolio size.

Bottom line: large multifamily operators focused on revenue optimization and leasing performance pick RealPage; anyone with mixed property types, investment management needs, or a smaller portfolio picks Yardi.
comparisons.one_liner: RealPage is the multifamily revenue-optimization specialist; Yardi is the broader platform for every property type and size.

faq.question: Is RealPage only for multifamily properties?
faq.answer: Effectively, yes. RealPage's entire suite, from OneSite to revenue management to DemandX, targets multifamily and rental housing, and it has limited commercial CRE features. Yardi covers multifamily plus commercial, affordable housing, senior living, and coworking, making it the clear choice for mixed portfolios.

faq.question: Can small landlords use RealPage or Yardi?
faq.answer: RealPage is enterprise-priced and not suitable for small landlords or single properties. Yardi serves small operators through Yardi Breeze, which starts at a published $1/unit/month. If you have a small portfolio, Yardi Breeze is the realistic option between these two.

faq.question: What is the concern with RealPage's revenue management?
faq.answer: RealPage's revenue management pricing algorithms have faced DOJ antitrust scrutiny. The product itself is considered industry-leading for optimizing multifamily rents, but buyers should weigh the legal and reputational risk as part of due diligence before adopting it.

comparisons.verdict:
This comparison is really about how big and complicated your operation is. Buildium is purpose-built residential property management software with transparent pricing: published plans at $62, $192, and $400 per month, a free trial, and a deep feature set covering leasing, screening, accounting, maintenance, and community associations for portfolios from a handful of doors up to 15,000+ units. Yardi is a full real estate platform spanning every property type, with Breeze (from $1/unit/month) at the low end and enterprise-grade Voyager, investment management, and energy suites at the top.

Buildium wins on simplicity and transparency. You can see the price, start a free trial, and be running without an implementation project; its Lumina AI handles bill scanning and communications, and it covers niches like community associations and student housing well. Its limits: it is primarily residential with thin commercial capability, and API access is locked to the $400/month Premium tier. Yardi wins the moment you need commercial management, fund accounting, investor portals, or a platform that scales into institutional territory, though Voyager brings a steep learning curve and lengthy implementations.

Bottom line: residential managers and landlords who want transparent pricing and fast setup pick Buildium; mixed or institutional portfolios that will grow into commercial and investment management pick Yardi.
comparisons.one_liner: Buildium for straightforward residential management with transparent pricing; Yardi when you need commercial, investment, or enterprise scale.

faq.question: Is Buildium cheaper than Yardi?
faq.answer: Buildium is the more transparent of the two, with published plans at $62, $192, and $400 per month and a free trial. Yardi Breeze starts at $1/unit/month, which can be cheaper for small unit counts, while Yardi Voyager is quote-based enterprise pricing. Actual cost depends on your portfolio size and the features you need.

faq.question: Can Buildium handle commercial properties?
faq.answer: Only in a limited way. Buildium supports mixed portfolios and lists commercial among its property types, but it is purpose-built for residential management and its commercial features are thin. Yardi has dedicated commercial management capability and is the better choice if commercial assets are a meaningful part of your business.

faq.question: Which is better for a small landlord, Buildium or Yardi?
faq.answer: Both are viable. Buildium's Essential plan at $62/month with a free trial is easy to evaluate, while Yardi Breeze's $1/unit/month can be very cheap for small portfolios. Buildium offers the deeper residential feature set; Breeze offers simplicity and a growth path into the larger Yardi ecosystem.

comparisons.verdict:
AppFolio and Buildium are the two most common shortlist rivals for residential property managers, and the split is fairly clean. Buildium is the accessible option: published pricing from $62/month up to $400/month for Premium, a free trial, and an all-in-one feature set spanning leasing, screening, accounting, maintenance, community associations, and student housing, serving everyone from individual landlords to 15,000+ unit portfolios. AppFolio positions itself upmarket as an AI-native 'Performance Platform' for managers from roughly 50 units to 14,000+, with agentic AI and its Realm-X Flows engine automating work across leasing, accounting, and maintenance.

Buildium wins on transparency and low-end accessibility: you know the price, you can trial it, and small landlords are squarely in its target market. Its AI (Lumina) is solid for bill scanning and communications, though API access requires the Premium tier. AppFolio wins on automation ambition and unified workflow for growing professional operations, and it adds investment management tools Buildium lacks. The trade-offs are quote-based premium pricing, no published numbers, and a platform that may be more than small operators need.

Bottom line: individual landlords and small-to-mid residential managers pick Buildium; professional firms at 50+ units betting on AI-driven operations and investor reporting pick AppFolio.
comparisons.one_liner: Buildium wins for small landlords with transparent $62+/month pricing; AppFolio suits growth-minded firms wanting deeper AI automation.

faq.question: Is AppFolio more expensive than Buildium?
faq.answer: AppFolio does not publish pricing; it is quote-based and generally positioned as premium for its AI capabilities. Buildium publishes plans at $62, $192, and $400 per month with a free trial. For small portfolios Buildium is the more predictable spend; at larger scale you will need an AppFolio quote to compare.

faq.question: Can I use AppFolio or Buildium as a small landlord with a few units?
faq.answer: Buildium is the better fit; it explicitly serves solo landlords and its Essential plan starts at $62/month with a free trial. AppFolio targets professional managers starting around 50 units, so very small portfolios are outside its sweet spot.

faq.question: Which has better AI features, AppFolio or Buildium?
faq.answer: Both invest heavily in AI. AppFolio's differentiator is agentic AI built into the platform core with the Realm-X Flows automation engine, aimed at automating whole workflows. Buildium's Lumina AI covers communications, writing assistance, and bill scanning. AppFolio's automation is more ambitious; Buildium's is more accessible, though its full AI suite sits in higher tiers.

comparisons.verdict:
These two rarely serve the same buyer, so the choice usually makes itself. AppFolio is a cloud-only, AI-native platform for residential property managers, from roughly 50 units to 14,000+, with agentic AI, the Realm-X Flows workflow engine, and a unified interface covering property and investment management. MRI Software is an enterprise real estate platform with 50+ years of history and 50,000+ clients, built for commercial and mixed-use portfolios: commercial lease administration, AI lease abstraction, fund and investment management, and the Angus facilities platform, all on an open architecture with 200+ integration partners.

AppFolio wins for residential operators who want modern software that reduces busywork; its AI is native rather than retrofitted, and everything lives in one interface on any device. It has little to offer a commercial landlord, though. MRI wins for commercial and institutional buyers: lease intelligence, facilities management, and investor reporting at a depth AppFolio does not attempt, plus the freedom to plug in best-of-breed tools like VTS and ARGUS. The costs are complexity, quote-based enterprise pricing, lengthy implementations, and some inconsistency across acquired products.

Bottom line: residential property management firms pick AppFolio; commercial, mixed-use, and institutional portfolios pick MRI. If you genuinely straddle both, MRI covers residential too, but AppFolio cannot cover serious commercial.
comparisons.one_liner: AppFolio for AI-driven residential management; MRI for commercial, mixed-use, and institutional portfolios needing enterprise depth.

faq.question: Can AppFolio manage commercial real estate like MRI?
faq.answer: Not at MRI's level. AppFolio lists commercial among supported property types but is built for residential managers. MRI offers full-stack commercial management including lease administration, AI-powered lease abstraction, and facilities management via MRI Angus. Commercial-focused buyers should look to MRI.

faq.question: How do AppFolio and MRI pricing compare?
faq.answer: Both are quote-based with no published prices, so you will need sales conversations either way. AppFolio is positioned as premium pricing for residential portfolios; MRI is enterprise pricing aimed at mid-market and large organizations. Neither offers a free trial or free tier.

faq.question: Which is easier to adopt, AppFolio or MRI?
faq.answer: AppFolio, for its audience. It is a single cloud platform with a unified interface, though its AI-native approach still requires some change management. MRI is a broad enterprise platform with a steep learning curve, potentially lengthy implementations, and user experiences that vary across its acquired products.

comparisons.verdict:
Both of these platforms chase residential operators with heavy AI investment, but at different altitudes. AppFolio serves property management companies from about 50 units to 14,000+, wrapping property management, investment management, and agentic AI automation into one unified cloud experience. RealPage is aimed at mid-market and enterprise multifamily: OneSite property management, Knock CRM, G5 advertising, DemandX demand forecasting, utility and spend management, and its flagship AI-driven revenue management, used by some of the world's largest apartment operators.

AppFolio wins on unified experience and accessibility for professional management firms; one platform, one login, with AI woven through leasing, accounting, and maintenance rather than assembled from acquisitions. RealPage wins on enterprise multifamily firepower: no one in this matchup matches its revenue optimization, market analytics footprint, and marketing stack. The trade-offs are steep on both sides. RealPage is enterprise-priced, complex to learn, and its revenue management algorithms carry active DOJ antitrust scrutiny. AppFolio is quote-based premium pricing and lacks RealPage's revenue management and market data depth.

Bottom line: property management companies in the tens-to-thousands of units pick AppFolio for its unified AI platform; large institutional multifamily operators who live and die by occupancy and rent optimization pick RealPage.
comparisons.one_liner: AppFolio for unified AI-native management at mid-scale; RealPage for enterprise multifamily revenue optimization and analytics.

faq.question: Is AppFolio or RealPage better for a mid-sized property management company?
faq.answer: AppFolio targets exactly that range, roughly 50 to 14,000+ units, with a single unified platform. RealPage is built for mid-market and enterprise multifamily operators and is not suitable for smaller portfolios. Most mid-sized third-party management firms will find AppFolio the more natural fit.

faq.question: How much do AppFolio and RealPage cost?
faq.answer: Neither publishes pricing; both are quote-based with no free trial. AppFolio is positioned as premium pricing for its AI capabilities, and RealPage as enterprise pricing. Expect sales-led purchasing processes with both, and get quotes scoped to your unit count and modules.

faq.question: Does AppFolio have revenue management like RealPage?
faq.answer: No. RealPage's AI-driven revenue management, which optimizes pricing against supply and demand, is its signature capability, alongside market analytics and the DemandX forecasting platform. AppFolio's AI focuses on automating operational busywork and performance insights rather than algorithmic rent pricing. Note that RealPage's pricing algorithms have drawn DOJ antitrust scrutiny.

comparisons.verdict:
This is the widest gap of any pairing here; these products serve almost entirely different buyers. Buildium is residential property management software with published pricing from $62/month to $400/month, a free trial, and an all-in-one toolkit for landlords, property managers, and community association managers running anywhere from a few doors to 15,000+ units. RealPage is an enterprise multifamily platform, quote-based and sales-led, offering OneSite property management, Knock CRM, AI-driven revenue management, DemandX demand forecasting, and utility and spend management for some of the largest apartment operators in the world.

Buildium wins on everything a small or mid-sized operator cares about: transparent pricing, fast self-serve setup, community association support, and features like Lumina AI bill scanning without an enterprise contract. RealPage wins on everything an institutional multifamily operator cares about: revenue optimization, market benchmarking data, fraud detection, and a marketing stack. RealPage is explicitly not suitable for small landlords, carries a steep learning curve, and its revenue management algorithms have drawn DOJ antitrust scrutiny. Buildium, for its part, cannot offer revenue management or enterprise analytics.

Bottom line: landlords, small-to-mid property managers, and HOA managers pick Buildium without hesitation; institutional multifamily portfolios optimizing thousands of units pick RealPage. Few buyers should genuinely be torn.
comparisons.one_liner: Buildium serves landlords and SMB managers with transparent pricing; RealPage serves institutional multifamily. Almost no overlap.

faq.question: Is Buildium cheaper than RealPage?
faq.answer: Almost certainly, for the buyers who could use either. Buildium publishes plans at $62, $192, and $400 per month with a free trial. RealPage is quote-based enterprise pricing with no published numbers and no trial, and it is explicitly not aimed at small landlords or single properties.

faq.question: Can Buildium do revenue management like RealPage?
faq.answer: No. RealPage's AI-driven revenue management and market analytics are enterprise multifamily tools with no equivalent in Buildium. Buildium's automation focuses on operations: rent collection, late fees, communications, bill scanning, and workflow rules. If algorithmic rent optimization is the goal, RealPage is the only option of the two.

faq.question: When should a growing property manager move from Buildium to RealPage?
faq.answer: Buildium supports portfolios up to 15,000+ units, so unit count alone rarely forces a move. The switch makes sense when you become an institutional multifamily operator needing revenue management, market benchmarking, and demand forecasting, and can absorb enterprise pricing and a complex implementation.

comparisons.verdict:
Both are enterprise platforms with quote-based pricing and real learning curves, so this decision comes down to what you own. RealPage is a multifamily specialist: OneSite property management, Knock CRM, G5 advertising, DemandX forecasting, and the industry's best-known AI revenue management, all built for apartment operators at mid-market and enterprise scale. MRI Software is a generalist with deep commercial roots: 50+ years in market, 50,000+ clients, commercial lease administration, AI lease abstraction, investment and fund management, and the Angus facilities platform, delivered on an open architecture with 200+ integration partners.

RealPage wins for multifamily operators, full stop. Its revenue optimization, market data footprint, and Lumina AI workforce target apartment economics in a way MRI does not, though buyers should weigh the DOJ antitrust scrutiny around its pricing algorithms. MRI wins for commercial, mixed-use, and investment-driven organizations: lease intelligence, investor reporting with waterfall modeling, and facilities management are core strengths, and its open platform plays well with tools like VTS and ARGUS. MRI also covers residential, making it the safer pick for genuinely mixed portfolios, though product sprawl from acquisitions can mean uneven user experiences.

Bottom line: enterprise multifamily operators pick RealPage; commercial, mixed-use, and investment management organizations pick MRI.
comparisons.one_liner: RealPage for enterprise multifamily revenue optimization; MRI for commercial, mixed-use, and investment management depth.

faq.question: Does RealPage work for commercial real estate?
faq.answer: Not really. RealPage is focused on multifamily and rental housing, with limited commercial CRE features. MRI offers full-stack commercial management including lease administration, AI lease abstraction, and facilities management, and it handles residential too, making it the choice for commercial or mixed portfolios.

faq.question: How do RealPage and MRI compare on price?
faq.answer: Both are quote-based enterprise platforms with no published pricing, free trials, or free tiers, so you will need scoped quotes from each. Neither is accessible to small firms; both target mid-market and enterprise organizations.

faq.question: Which platform integrates better with other software?
faq.answer: MRI is explicitly built as an open platform with 200+ integration partners, including VTS, ARGUS, and DocuSign, so best-of-breed stacks are a design goal. RealPage's strength is the breadth of its own ecosystem (Knock, G5, DemandX) rather than openness, though it does integrate with partners like Plaid and even Yardi.

comparisons.verdict:
This is less a rivalry than a question of layer; in fact, VTS lists MRI as an integration partner, and plenty of landlords run both. MRI is a system of record: commercial and residential property management, real estate accounting, lease administration, investment and fund management, and facilities via MRI Angus, serving 50,000+ clients on an open platform with 200+ integrations. VTS is a system of action for commercial leasing and asset management: deal pipeline tracking, AI proposal generation, tenant relationship intelligence, digital marketing, tenant experience via VTS Activate, and market intelligence powered by data on 13B+ square feet under management.

VTS wins wherever leasing velocity and market insight matter: real-time deal visibility across a portfolio, proposals generated dramatically faster with Proposal AI, and predictive office demand data (VODI, VTS Analyst) that MRI does not offer. It does not do accounting or property-level financials, so it cannot replace MRI. MRI wins as the operational and financial backbone, with lease abstraction, investor reporting, and facilities management. Both carry enterprise, quote-based pricing and learning curves; VTS is also primarily office and commercial focused, with newer multifamily capability.

Bottom line: commercial landlords needing accounting and lease administration pick MRI; leasing and asset management teams chasing deal velocity pick VTS; large office portfolios frequently deploy VTS on top of MRI.
comparisons.one_liner: Not either/or: MRI is the accounting and lease-admin backbone; VTS is the leasing and market-intelligence layer, and they integrate.

faq.question: Can VTS replace MRI Software?
faq.answer: No. VTS covers leasing workflow, deal pipeline, marketing, tenant experience, and market data, but it is not an accounting or lease administration system of record. MRI provides the GL, AP/AR, lease admin, and investor reporting a landlord's back office runs on. Many firms use VTS for leasing on top of MRI.

faq.question: Do VTS and MRI integrate with each other?
faq.answer: Yes. VTS lists MRI Software as an accounting integration partner, and MRI lists VTS as a leasing partner on its open platform of 200+ integrations. Running VTS as the leasing layer over MRI as the system of record is a common enterprise setup.

faq.question: How much do VTS and MRI cost?
faq.answer: Both are quote-based with no published pricing, and both are enterprise products; VTS in particular is not priced for small brokerages or individual brokers. Expect sales-led processes and costs scoped to portfolio size and modules for either platform.

comparisons.verdict:
VTS and Yardi solve different problems that happen to overlap. VTS is a leasing and asset management platform: deal pipeline tracking, AI proposal generation, tenant relationship intelligence, digital marketing, and market data built on 13B+ square feet under management. Yardi is the operational and accounting backbone, covering property management, full general ledger accounting, investment management, and fund accounting across multifamily, commercial, affordable housing, and senior living. Tellingly, VTS lists Yardi as an accounting integration; many large landlords run both.

VTS wins on leasing workflow and market intelligence. Its Proposal AI, lease roll management, and VTS Data products are built for landlords and brokers who live in the deal cycle, and nothing in Yardi's stack matches its office demand data. Yardi wins on breadth and operational depth: it is a single stack for operations, accounting, and investment management, serves every property type, and Yardi Breeze starts at $1/unit/month, giving smaller operators an entry point VTS's enterprise, quote-based pricing does not.

Bottom line: choose Yardi if you need core property management and accounting, especially across mixed portfolios. Choose VTS if your system of record is settled and you need to modernize leasing, asset management, and tenant experience. Large office landlords often justify both; small operators should start with Yardi Breeze, since VTS is not priced for them.
comparisons.one_liner: Yardi is the property management and accounting backbone; VTS is the leasing and asset management layer that often sits on top of it.

faq.question: Can VTS replace Yardi?
faq.answer: Generally no. VTS covers leasing, asset management, marketing, and tenant experience but is not a full accounting and property management system, while Yardi provides the general ledger, AP/AR, and operational core. VTS actually integrates with Yardi, and many large landlords run the two together.

faq.question: Which is better for a small landlord or brokerage?
faq.answer: Yardi, through Yardi Breeze, which starts at $1/unit/month and is built for smaller portfolios. VTS is enterprise-focused with quote-based pricing and is not accessible for small brokerages or individual brokers.

faq.question: How do VTS and Yardi pricing compare?
faq.answer: Yardi publishes entry pricing for Breeze ($1/unit/month, $2 for Premier) while its enterprise Voyager platform is quote-based. VTS does not publish pricing at all; expect a sales conversation and enterprise-level contracts for either flagship product.

comparisons.verdict:
Argus and Dealpath sit at different points in the investment workflow. Argus, by Altus Group, is the industry-standard valuation engine: discounted cash flow modeling, cash flow projections, and investment analysis, taught in over 200 universities and recognized by investors, appraisers, and lenders globally. Dealpath is deal management: a pipeline and execution platform that centralizes every active deal, automates due diligence and IC approval workflows, and uses AI to extract data from OMs and flyers. Trusted by 300+ firms including top-tier institutional investors, it is the system of record for how deals move, not how they are valued.

Argus wins wherever rigorous property-level valuation is the job, and its DCF depth is unmatched, though it carries a steep learning curve and a dated interface. Dealpath wins on team workflow: real-time pipeline visibility, side-by-side underwriting comparison, white-glove implementation, and a built-in CRM for brokers and JV partners. It requires a five-user minimum and a 6-8 week implementation, so it is not for solo practitioners.

Bottom line: these are complements more than competitors. Appraisers, underwriters, and analysts who need defensible valuations need Argus. Acquisitions teams drowning in spreadsheet pipelines and email-based deal tracking need Dealpath. Institutional investment shops typically end up with both, since both are quote-based enterprise purchases.
comparisons.one_liner: Argus is the industry-standard DCF valuation engine; Dealpath manages the deal pipeline around it. Most institutional teams need both.

faq.question: Do Argus and Dealpath do the same thing?
faq.answer: No. Argus is valuation and cash flow forecasting software for analyzing individual properties, while Dealpath tracks and executes the deal pipeline itself, from sourcing through close. Many acquisitions teams model in Argus and manage the process in Dealpath.

faq.question: Which is right for a small investment firm?
faq.answer: Neither is a natural fit for very small shops. Argus carries enterprise pricing and a steep learning curve, and Dealpath requires a minimum of five users with a 6-8 week implementation. Dealpath itself is best suited to institutional investors and can be over-engineered for smaller owner-operators.

faq.question: How much do Argus and Dealpath cost?
faq.answer: Both are quote-based, and neither publishes pricing. Dealpath is subscription-based with multiple tiers and a five-user minimum; Argus is sold through Altus Group on custom terms. Budget for enterprise-level contracts and sales conversations with each.

comparisons.verdict:
Argus and Juniper Square serve adjacent but distinct layers of the institutional real estate stack. Argus is property-level analysis: the industry-standard DCF modeling, cash flow projection, and investment analysis tool used by analysts, appraisers, and asset managers to value assets and underwrite deals. Juniper Square is the investor-facing layer: fundraising, investor onboarding, an LP portal, compliance, treasury, and full fund administration services, serving over 2,000 GPs with $1 trillion in investor equity and 700,000+ investor accounts.

Argus wins on valuation rigor. Its DCF depth is unmatched, it is taught in 200+ universities, and lenders and investors recognize its outputs. Its weaknesses are a steep learning curve and legacy desktop roots. Juniper Square wins on everything after capital is raised: complex fund structure administration, automated compliance and reporting, and its JunieAI layer for workflow automation. Its weaknesses are the mirror image, since it does no property-level valuation and is focused on private markets fund operations rather than asset analysis.

Bottom line: this is rarely an either/or choice. If you are valuing buildings and underwriting acquisitions, buy Argus. If you are raising funds, managing LPs, and running fund accounting, buy Juniper Square. A GP running commingled funds will likely need both. Both are quote-based enterprise products aimed at mid-market and enterprise firms.
comparisons.one_liner: Argus values the assets; Juniper Square manages the fund and its investors. GPs running institutional capital typically need both layers.

faq.question: Does Juniper Square do valuation or underwriting like Argus?
faq.answer: No. Juniper Square is built for fundraising, investor management, and fund administration, not property-level DCF modeling. Argus remains the industry standard for valuation and cash flow forecasting, and the two address different stages of the investment lifecycle.

faq.question: Which should a new fund manager buy first?
faq.answer: It depends on the bottleneck. If you are underwriting deals, Argus (or an analyst who knows it) comes first. If you are raising outside capital and onboarding LPs, Juniper Square's fundraising, portal, and administration tools matter more, though its enterprise pricing may be high for smaller fund managers.

faq.question: How is each product priced?
