faq.answer: Both are quote-based with no published prices. Juniper Square pricing is customized based on AUM and requirements; Argus is sold by Altus Group on enterprise terms. Neither offers a free trial or free tier.

comparisons.verdict:
Dealpath and Juniper Square both serve institutional real estate investment firms, but on opposite sides of the house. Dealpath is for the acquisitions team: a deal management platform with real-time pipeline tracking, AI-powered extraction of OM and flyer data, due diligence and IC approval workflows, and side-by-side underwriting comparison, trusted by 300+ firms including Blackstone and CBRE IM. Juniper Square is for investor relations and fund operations: fundraising, LP onboarding, an investor portal, compliance, treasury, and full fund administration, serving 2,000+ GPs managing $1 trillion in investor equity.

Dealpath wins on deal execution, with a purpose-built workflow from sourcing to close, strong data integrations (CompStak, Esri, RCA), and white-glove implementation. Its limits are a five-user minimum and a scope that stops at deal management, since it is not an accounting or fund administration system. Juniper Square wins after the capital is raised, handling complex fund structures, automated compliance reporting, and LP communications, with JunieAI layered across workflows. Its limits are the mirror image: it does not manage your acquisitions pipeline.

Bottom line: buy Dealpath if your pain is deal flow chaos and your acquisitions team lives in spreadsheets. Buy Juniper Square if your pain is investor reporting, fundraising, and fund accounting. Vertically integrated GPs frequently need both, and both are quote-based enterprise purchases.
comparisons.one_liner: Dealpath runs the acquisitions pipeline; Juniper Square runs fundraising and fund administration. They cover opposite sides of a GP's business.

faq.question: Do Dealpath and Juniper Square overlap at all?
faq.answer: Very little. Dealpath manages deals from sourcing through close, including due diligence and IC approvals, while Juniper Square manages investors, fundraising, and fund administration. A firm that acquires assets and manages outside capital would use them for different teams.

faq.question: Which is better for a small real estate investment team?
faq.answer: Both skew institutional. Dealpath requires a minimum of five users and is best suited to institutional investors, and Juniper Square's enterprise-level pricing may be high for smaller fund managers. Very small teams should weigh whether the workflow gains justify enterprise contracts.

faq.question: What do Dealpath and Juniper Square cost?
faq.answer: Neither publishes pricing. Dealpath is subscription-based with custom quotes and a 6-8 week implementation; Juniper Square is quote-based with pricing tied to AUM and requirements. Plan for sales conversations with both.

comparisons.verdict:
CoStar and CompStak both sell CRE comp data, but they gather it in fundamentally different ways. CoStar employs a research team of 1,000+ professionals to maintain the largest US commercial property database, covering 6 million+ properties with ownership records, lease and sales comps, tenant data, CMBS/loan data, and submarket analytics, serving 150,000+ professionals. CompStak crowdsources: its 35,000+ member network of appraisers, brokers, and researchers trades authenticated comps for database access, producing granular deal-level detail like effective rent, TI allowances, free rent, and escalations that CoStar does not surface.

CoStar wins on breadth. It is the comprehensive market view, with property-level records, forecasting models, tenant prospecting, and LoopNet marketplace reach. The costs are premium pricing that shuts out smaller firms, annual contracts, and a steep learning curve. CompStak wins on lease economics depth and on price: brokers and appraisers who contribute their own comps get access free through the exchange. Its tradeoffs are contribution-dependent data quality that can be uneven in smaller markets, and a smaller overall dataset with no building operations data.

Bottom line: institutional shops that need the full market picture buy CoStar, and often add CompStak for true effective rents on specific deals. Brokers and appraisers with comps to trade should start with CompStak's free exchange before committing to a CoStar contract.
comparisons.one_liner: CoStar is the comprehensive researched database; CompStak trades crowdsourced comps for unmatched effective-rent detail. Often free for contributors.

faq.question: Is CompStak data as reliable as CoStar's?
faq.answer: They have different strengths. CoStar's 1,000+ person research team ensures consistent breadth and timeliness, while CompStak's authenticated member-contributed comps offer deal-level detail like effective rent, TI, and free rent that CoStar lacks. CompStak's coverage can be uneven in smaller markets where fewer members contribute.

faq.question: Can I get CompStak for free?
faq.answer: Yes, if you have comps to trade. CompStak's exchange model lets appraisers, brokers, and researchers contribute their own deal data to earn credits for accessing the database. Institutional users who cannot contribute comps pay for the Enterprise platform, which is quote-based.

faq.question: Do firms use CoStar and CompStak together?
faq.answer: Commonly, yes. CoStar provides the broad market overview, property records, and analytics, while CompStak fills in granular lease economics for underwriting and appraisal work. CompStak explicitly positions its data as complementary detail that is difficult to find elsewhere.

comparisons.verdict:
CoStar and Placer.ai answer different questions about the same properties. CoStar tells you what a property is and what it trades for: ownership, tenancy, lease and sales comps, vacancy, absorption, and rent forecasts across 6 million+ US commercial properties, backed by a 1,000+ person research team. Placer.ai tells you how a location actually performs in the physical world: foot traffic trends, visitor demographics, true trade areas based on where visitors live and work, dwell time, cross-shopping behavior, and competitive benchmarking, from a de-identified mobile panel it reports at 92%+ accuracy.

CoStar wins as the general-purpose CRE data platform, since no rival matches its breadth across office, industrial, retail, and multifamily or its transaction and market analytics. Placer wins for retail-oriented decisions like site selection, tenant health assessment, and trade area analysis, where lease comps alone cannot tell you whether a center is actually drawing customers. Placer also has a free dashboard tier, a rarity in CRE data, while CoStar's premium pricing and annual contracts are a known barrier for smaller firms. Placer's limits are US-focused coverage and lower relevance for pure office or industrial plays.

Bottom line: investors and brokers who need comps, ownership data, and market analytics need CoStar. Retail investors, site selection teams, and anyone underwriting tenant performance should use Placer, starting with the free tier. For retail acquisitions, the two are genuinely complementary.
comparisons.one_liner: CoStar covers property data and comps; Placer.ai measures real-world foot traffic. Retail buyers often want both, and Placer has a free tier.

faq.question: Does Placer.ai replace CoStar for retail investors?
faq.answer: No. Placer provides foot traffic, visitor demographics, and trade area analysis, but not lease comps, sales transactions, or ownership records, which is CoStar's territory. For retail underwriting they answer complementary questions: CoStar covers the deal economics, Placer covers whether customers actually show up.

faq.question: Is Placer.ai really free?
faq.answer: There is a genuinely useful free dashboard with basic foot traffic data and limited property lookups. Full analytics, trade area analysis, API access, and data feeds require paid Professional or Enterprise plans, which are quote-based and can be expensive.

faq.question: Which is better for office or industrial properties?
faq.answer: CoStar, clearly. Its database covers all major property types with submarket-level analytics. Placer's foot traffic data is most valuable for retail, hospitality, and entertainment; it is less relevant for pure office or industrial assets.

comparisons.verdict:
CompStak and Placer.ai are both alternative data plays, but they measure entirely different things. CompStak is transaction data: crowdsourced, authenticated lease and sales comps from a 35,000+ member network of appraisers and brokers, with granular detail like effective rent, TI, free rent, cap rates, and lease expirations across US markets. Placer.ai is behavioral data: foot traffic, visitor demographics, trade areas, dwell time, and cross-shopping patterns for any physical US location, drawn from a mobile panel it reports at 92%+ accuracy.

CompStak wins for valuation and underwriting work, since appraisers and institutional investors use it because its effective rent detail is hard to find anywhere else, and contributors can access it free through the exchange model. Its data quality depends on member contributions and can thin out in smaller markets. Placer wins for retail-oriented questions such as whether a tenant is drawing customers, where a center's trade area really extends, and how a site compares to competitors. It offers a free dashboard tier plus a strong API, but is less relevant for pure office or industrial analysis.

Bottom line: this is rarely a head-to-head choice. Appraisers and lease-focused analysts need CompStak; retail investors and site selection teams need Placer. If you are underwriting a shopping center, the strongest position is CompStak for the rent roll economics and Placer for the customer traffic, and both offer free entry points worth testing first.
comparisons.one_liner: CompStak delivers granular lease and sales comps; Placer.ai delivers foot traffic and trade areas. Different data for different questions.

faq.question: Do CompStak and Placer.ai compete with each other?
faq.answer: Not really. CompStak provides lease and sales transaction comps for valuation and underwriting, while Placer provides foot traffic and consumer behavior analytics for site selection and tenant performance. A retail investor might use both on the same deal for different parts of the analysis.

faq.question: Which has a better free option?
faq.answer: Both have real free paths. CompStak is free for brokers and appraisers who contribute their own comps through its exchange model, while Placer offers a free dashboard with basic foot traffic data for anyone. Enterprise access to either is quote-based.

faq.question: Which is more useful for office properties?
faq.answer: CompStak. Its lease comps, effective rents, and expiration data cover office markets in depth, whereas Placer's foot traffic data is most valuable for retail, hospitality, and entertainment locations and less relevant for pure office analysis.

comparisons.verdict:
HqO and SmartRent both live under the tenant experience banner, but they serve different asset classes with different tools. HqO is built for commercial office and mixed-use: a Real Estate Experience platform positioning itself as the first CRM purpose-built for CRE, with AI-powered portfolio analytics, programmable building experiences, amenity management, and access control aimed at landlords trying to keep office tenants engaged and renewing. SmartRent is built for multifamily: smart home hardware plus cloud software, including smart locks, access control, self-guided tours, community WiFi, and parking management, deployed across 600+ clients, 1.3M rental homes, and 3.5M connected devices.

HqO wins for office landlords, since its Intelligence Suite measures tenant engagement and experience outcomes across a portfolio, which is something SmartRent does not attempt for commercial tenants. It is enterprise-focused and may be complex for smaller landlords. SmartRent wins for multifamily operators on operational ROI, with its data citing $30-60 in added value per unit per month, and its self-guided tours and IoT maintenance tools directly reducing staffing load. It does require upfront hardware investment and installation.

Bottom line: the choice is made by your portfolio. Office and mixed-use landlords should look at HqO; multifamily operators should look at SmartRent. There is little reason to cross-shop them, and if you hold both asset types, expect to run different platforms for each. Both are quote-based.
comparisons.one_liner: HqO is tenant experience for office portfolios; SmartRent is smart-home hardware and software for multifamily. Pick by asset class.

faq.question: Can SmartRent be used for commercial office buildings?
faq.answer: SmartRent is designed for multifamily communities and rental properties, including student housing and senior living, with hardware like smart locks and community WiFi. It is not built for commercial office tenant engagement, which is exactly where HqO focuses.

faq.question: What ROI can I expect from each platform?
faq.answer: SmartRent's materials cite $30-60 in added value per unit per month from smart home amenities and operational savings, plus revenue from parking monetization. HqO frames its value as measurable tenant experience outcomes and engagement analytics; specific pricing and ROI figures are quote-based for both.

faq.question: Does either platform require hardware?
faq.answer: SmartRent does. It is a hardware-plus-software model with smart devices, hubs, and installation, which means upfront investment and ongoing device maintenance. HqO is primarily a software platform, though it integrates with building systems like access control.

comparisons.verdict:
CoStar and Crexi compete most directly in listings and marketplaces, but they are different-sized bets. CoStar is the incumbent: the largest US commercial property database with 6 million+ properties, verified lease and sales comps, forecasting, tenant prospecting, and marketplace reach through LoopNet and Apartments.com, maintained by a 1,000+ person research team and used by 150,000+ professionals. Crexi is the challenger: a fast-growing marketplace with 500,000+ active listings and $4T+ in property value, combining listings, deal management, and Crexi Intelligence analytics in a modern interface, with a genuinely free tier for basic listing and search.

CoStar wins on data depth and institutional reach. Its comps, analytics, and research are the industry benchmark, and LoopNet remains the most-visited CRE marketplace. The price is premium pricing, annual contracts, and complexity that can overwhelm users who just need property search. Crexi wins on accessibility and usability: free basic access, a modern mobile experience, and no annual lock-in at the entry level. Its listing inventory is smaller in some markets, its data depth is still maturing, and institutional players still default to CoStar.

Bottom line: institutional brokers, investors, appraisers, and lenders who need verified comps and analytics should pay for CoStar. Independent brokers and smaller shops marketing listings should start with Crexi's free tier and upgrade as needed. Many brokers list on both to maximize exposure.
comparisons.one_liner: CoStar/LoopNet is the data-rich institutional standard; Crexi is the free-to-start, modern challenger. Many brokers simply use both.

faq.question: Is Crexi a real alternative to CoStar and LoopNet?
faq.answer: For listing and marketing properties, yes. Crexi has 500,000+ active listings and has become a top LoopNet alternative with a modern interface and free basic access. For research-grade comps, ownership data, and analytics, CoStar's database remains substantially deeper.

faq.question: What does each platform cost?
faq.answer: Crexi offers a free tier for basic listings and search, with Pro and Enterprise subscriptions quoted by sales. CoStar is subscription-based with premium, quote-based pricing and annual contracts, which its own critics note can be cost-prohibitive for smaller firms and individual brokers.

faq.question: Should I list my property on both?
faq.answer: If budget allows, exposure argues for it. LoopNet brings the largest audience while Crexi is free to start and growing fast. Solo brokers on a budget can begin with Crexi's free listings and add paid syndication where a specific market demands it.

comparisons.verdict:
This comparison has an unusual asterisk: Apto's website is no longer accessible, and the product appears to have been discontinued or acquired. Apto was a pioneer, one of the first CRMs purpose-built for CRE brokers, built on Salesforce with contact management, deal tracking, and commission management. But a CRM you may not be able to buy, or get supported, is not a viable choice for a new purchase, and existing Apto users likely face a migration decision.

Buildout is the active, growing alternative. Used by 50,000+ CRE brokers, it spans far more than CRM: AI-powered prospecting across a 40M+ property database, marketing with automated proposals and syndication to 20+ listing sites, the Rethink CRM with AI-assisted follow-up, and Transact for closing workflows. It is modular, so you can start with one product and expand, and it scales from solo brokers to multi-office brokerages. Its main caveats are quote-based pricing with no published numbers and some still-maturing AI features.

Bottom line: for anyone choosing a CRE brokerage platform today, Buildout is the practical answer, and Apto is effectively not an option. Former Apto users evaluating replacements will find Buildout's Rethink CRM covers the same broker-specific ground (contacts, pipeline, deal tracking) while adding prospecting and marketing Apto never had. Teams deeply invested in Salesforce infrastructure may want a Salesforce-native alternative, but that is a different search.
comparisons.one_liner: Apto appears discontinued; Buildout is the actively developed CRE brokerage platform and the practical choice. And a natural Apto migration path.

faq.question: Is Apto still available?
faq.answer: Apto's website is no longer accessible, suggesting the product was discontinued or acquired. That means limited or no ongoing support, and existing users should plan a migration to an actively maintained CRM rather than treating Apto as a current option.

faq.question: Is Buildout a good replacement for Apto?
faq.answer: Yes, for most former Apto users. Buildout's Rethink CRM covers CRE-specific contact management and deal pipeline tracking, and the wider platform adds AI prospecting, marketing with listing syndication, and transaction management that Apto did not offer. Note that Apto was Salesforce-based, so teams committed to Salesforce infrastructure should factor that into migration planning.

faq.question: How much does Buildout cost?
faq.answer: Buildout uses modular, quote-based pricing with no published prices; you can start with one product, such as the CRM or the Showcase marketing tool, and add others as needs grow. Expect a sales conversation to get numbers for your team size.

comparisons.verdict:
Crexi and LoopNet are both commercial real estate marketplaces, but they are built for different jobs. LoopNet, owned by CoStar Group, is the most visited CRE listing site in the United States, with over 10 million unique monthly visitors according to its published figures. It is primarily a listing and exposure platform. Crexi, founded in 2015, combines a marketplace with deal management, lead tracking, and its Crexi Intelligence analytics product. It positions itself as the alternative to LoopNet for brokers who want workflow tools alongside listings.

LoopNet wins on audience. Its listings rank highly in search, the brand is recognized by buyers and tenants, and institutional players default to it. Basic listings are free, and paid Gold, Platinum, and Diamond tiers add photography, video, 3D tours, and priority placement. Based on published pricing, those tiers run roughly $200 to $500 per listing per month. For a hard-to-move institutional asset in a major market, that exposure is often worth the cost.

Crexi wins on cost and workflow. Free basic access covers search and listings, and the Pro and Enterprise tiers, which are quote-based, add deal management, analytics, and lead tracking that LoopNet does not offer. Brokers who run a pipeline, not just a listing, get a single platform instead of a marketplace plus a separate CRM. The trade-offs are real: inventory is smaller than LoopNet in some markets, data depth is still maturing, and premium pricing is not public.

Pick LoopNet if maximum eyeballs on a listing is the goal and the marketing budget supports per-listing fees. Pick Crexi if you want deal management, analytics, and lower cost in one tool. Many brokerages use both: Crexi as the daily workspace, LoopNet paid tiers only for select properties.
comparisons.one_liner: LoopNet wins on raw listing exposure through CoStar's audience; Crexi wins on price, deal management, and a modern workflow for active brokers.

faq.question: Is LoopNet owned by CoStar?
faq.answer: Yes. LoopNet is owned by CoStar Group and serves as the public-facing marketplace that complements CoStar's professional data platform.

faq.question: Is Crexi free to use?
faq.answer: Crexi offers free basic access for property search and listings. Its Pro and Enterprise tiers, which add deal management, analytics, and Crexi Intelligence, are quote-based.

faq.question: Does LoopNet include deal management or CRM tools?
faq.answer: No. LoopNet is primarily a listing platform with limited CRM or deal management features. Crexi bundles deal flow management and lead tracking into its paid tiers.

faq.question: Which has more listings, Crexi or LoopNet?
faq.answer: LoopNet generally has the larger inventory and audience, especially in major institutional markets. Crexi's inventory is growing but remains smaller in some markets.

comparisons.verdict:
CoStar and Reonomy both sell commercial real estate data, but they answer different questions. CoStar maintains the largest CRE database in the United States, with building data, ownership, lease comps, sales transactions, and submarket analytics maintained by a research team of over 1,000 people. Reonomy, an Altus Group business since its 2021 acquisition, is a property intelligence platform. It stitches title, assessor, geospatial, and demographic records into unified property profiles using machine learning, with a focus on ownership and debt.

CoStar wins on depth and defensibility. Appraisers, lenders, and researchers who need lease comps, sales history, and market forecasts they can cite in a report will not find an equivalent in Reonomy, which has limited lease data. CoStar also covers all major property types at submarket granularity. The cost of that depth is premium pricing, annual contracts with limited flexibility, and a learning curve that overwhelms users who only need basic search.

Reonomy wins on prospecting. Its core strength is uncovering the true owner behind LLCs and trusts and surfacing contact details, plus mortgage and debt maturity data that flags likely sellers. Brokers building a call list or investors hunting off-market deals get to a usable target list faster than in CoStar. A free trial lowers the evaluation risk, though pricing is not published. Accuracy varies by market and is strongest in major metros.

Pick CoStar if your work depends on comps, valuation, or market analytics, and the budget supports an enterprise contract. Pick Reonomy if the job is finding and contacting owners. Firms that need both often pair a CoStar seat for research with Reonomy for the prospecting team, since the overlap between the two is smaller than it looks.
comparisons.one_liner: CoStar wins for lease comps, valuation, and market research; Reonomy wins for owner discovery and prospecting at a lower entry cost.

faq.question: Who owns Reonomy?
faq.answer: Reonomy has been owned by Altus Group, a Canadian real estate data and advisory company, since Altus acquired it in November 2021. It now operates as Reonomy, an Altus Group business.

faq.question: Does Reonomy have lease comps like CoStar?
faq.answer: Reonomy's lease data is limited compared to CoStar or CompStak. Its strengths are ownership records, contact information, and mortgage and debt maturity data used for prospecting.

faq.question: Is Reonomy cheaper than CoStar?
faq.answer: Reonomy's pricing is not published, so a direct comparison is not possible. Reonomy does offer a free trial, while CoStar is enterprise-priced on annual contracts.

faq.question: Can Reonomy replace CoStar?
faq.answer: Only for prospecting and ownership research. Teams that rely on CoStar for lease comps, sales comps, or market analytics will still need CoStar or another comps source.

comparisons.verdict:
Visual Lease and LeaseQuery both handle ASC 842, IFRS 16, and GASB 87 compliance, but they start from opposite ends of the lease lifecycle. Visual Lease, founded in 1996 and acquired by CoStar Group in November 2024, is a lease administration and accounting platform. It manages leases from acquisition to termination, covers both real estate and equipment, and connects real estate, finance, procurement, and legal teams around one record. LeaseQuery is the lease accounting product of FinQuery, the name its parent company adopted in February 2024 when it expanded into contract and spend management. It is built primarily for accountants.

Visual Lease wins when lease administration is the real job. Critical dates, options, CAM reconciliation inputs, and SOX-oriented controls live alongside the accounting entries, so corporate real estate and finance work from the same data. It integrates with SAP, Oracle, Workday, Microsoft Dynamics, and NetSuite, and now with CoStar market data. The trade-offs: pricing is enterprise-only on annual terms, implementations for complex global portfolios can be lengthy, some screens feel dated, and the CoStar acquisition may change pricing and product direction over time.

LeaseQuery wins on accounting focus and accessibility. It automates journal entries, disclosure reporting, and compliance workflows, and it serves small businesses through large enterprises. The FinQuery platform also covers prepaids and accruals, which matters for finance teams consolidating tools. It has strong onboarding support and integrations with NetSuite, SAP, Sage Intacct, QuickBooks, Dynamics, and Workday. Its limits are operational: it is not a lease administration system, so teams managing dates, renewals, and landlord relationships will need something else.

Pick Visual Lease if a corporate real estate or facilities team needs to run the portfolio, not just book it, and the organization is enterprise-scale. Pick LeaseQuery if the controller's office owns the project and the goal is clean, auditable compliance with the least operational overhead. Both are quote-based, so expect a sales conversation either way.
comparisons.one_liner: Visual Lease wins for enterprise lease administration across real estate and equipment; LeaseQuery, now part of FinQuery, wins for accounting-first compliance at any size.

faq.question: Is LeaseQuery the same company as FinQuery?
faq.answer: Yes. LeaseQuery rebranded its company as FinQuery in February 2024 to reflect expansion into contract and spend management. The lease accounting product itself still carries the LeaseQuery name.

faq.question: Who owns Visual Lease?
faq.answer: CoStar Group completed its acquisition of Visual Lease on November 1, 2024. Visual Lease now sits within CoStar's Real Estate Manager business line.

faq.question: Does LeaseQuery handle lease administration as well as accounting?
faq.answer: LeaseQuery is focused on lease accounting compliance. Its operational lease management features are limited compared to a dedicated lease administration platform like Visual Lease.

faq.question: Which lease accounting standards do Visual Lease and LeaseQuery support?
faq.answer: Both support ASC 842, IFRS 16, and GASB 87. Visual Lease also covers equipment leases alongside real estate, and FinQuery extends beyond leases into prepaids and accruals.

comparisons.verdict:
Entrata and RealPage are both enterprise property management platforms rooted in multifamily, but they differ in how they are assembled. Entrata is a single-vendor operating system: accounting, leasing, marketing, resident services, maintenance, and utilities run under one login, with its ELI layer adding AI across the platform. It reports over 32,000 properties and 3.2 million units across multifamily, student, affordable, military, commercial, and manufactured housing. RealPage is an integrated suite plus a data business. Its leasing, spend, utility, and resident tools sit alongside revenue management, DemandX demand forecasting, and the Lumina AI workforce, and it is used by some of the largest multifamily operators in the world.

Entrata wins on platform coherence and property-type reach. Operators tired of stitching together point solutions get one system without third-party dependencies, and the student, affordable, and military housing coverage is broader than RealPage's residential focus. The trade-offs: pricing is quote-based, the platform has a steep learning curve, commercial features are less mature than the multifamily core, and the closed ecosystem means fewer third-party integrations.

RealPage wins on analytics and revenue optimization. Its revenue management is the most established in the industry, its market data footprint supports benchmarking that Entrata cannot match, and Lumina automates tasks at scale. The trade-offs: enterprise-only pricing that excludes small landlords, a complex platform, a strictly multifamily orientation, and ongoing antitrust scrutiny from the Department of Justice around its revenue management pricing algorithms. That legal overhang is a real consideration for any operator making a long-term commitment.

Pick Entrata if you want one unified stack, especially with student, affordable, or military assets in the portfolio. Pick RealPage if revenue management and market analytics drive your operating model and you are comfortable with the regulatory questions around it. Both require sales conversations to establish pricing.
comparisons.one_liner: Entrata wins for operators who want one login across diverse housing types; RealPage wins for enterprise multifamily teams built around revenue management and analytics.

faq.question: Does RealPage work for commercial properties?
faq.answer: RealPage is focused on multifamily rental housing and has limited commercial features. Entrata lists commercial among its supported types, though its commercial tools are less mature than its multifamily core.

faq.question: Why is RealPage facing antitrust scrutiny?
faq.answer: The US Department of Justice has scrutinized RealPage's revenue management software over concerns that its pricing algorithms could coordinate rents across competing landlords. Operators should factor this into long-term platform decisions.

faq.question: Is Entrata cheaper than RealPage?
faq.answer: Neither vendor publishes pricing. Both are quote-based and aimed at mid-market and enterprise operators, so cost depends on portfolio size and modules.

faq.question: Can Entrata and RealPage work together?
faq.answer: Entrata lists RealPage among its analytics integrations, so some operators use RealPage data products alongside Entrata's operating platform. Entrata's ecosystem is otherwise relatively closed to third parties.

comparisons.verdict:
Entrata and Yardi both aim to run an entire property operation from one system, but Yardi spans far more of the real estate industry. Yardi's Voyager platform covers multifamily, commercial, affordable, senior living, coworking, and investment management, with clients in over 80 countries and a choice of cloud or on-premise deployment. Yardi Breeze serves smaller operators at a published price from $1 per unit per month, or $2 for Breeze Premier. Entrata is a multifamily-first operating system serving student, affordable, military, commercial, and manufactured housing as well, with one login across accounting, leasing, marketing, resident services, and maintenance, and its ELI AI layer throughout.

Yardi wins on breadth and flexibility. If the portfolio includes office, retail, or industrial assets, or needs fund accounting and an investor portal in the same stack, Entrata's commercial features are not as mature. Yardi's own ecosystem, including RentCafe, COMMERCIALCafe, and Yardi Matrix market data, extends the core, and Breeze gives small operators a genuine entry point. The costs are well documented: Voyager has a steep learning curve, implementations take months, some modules look dated, and migrating away later is hard.

Entrata wins on cohesion for multifamily operators. Everything is native to one platform with no third-party dependencies, the AI capabilities are integrated rather than added on, and it is proven at scale with over 32,000 properties. The trade-offs mirror Yardi's in places: quote-based pricing with no public tiers, a steep learning curve, and a closed ecosystem with fewer third-party integrations than some competitors.

Pick Yardi if the portfolio is mixed, international, or commercial-heavy, if on-premise deployment matters, or if you are small enough for Breeze. Pick Entrata if you run residential rental housing at scale and want a single modern platform without assembling modules. For multifamily-only operators the decision usually comes down to implementation experience and total cost from the sales process.
comparisons.one_liner: Yardi wins on property-type breadth, deployment options, and an affordable entry tier; Entrata wins for multifamily operators who want one modern, unified platform.

faq.question: Is Entrata or Yardi better for commercial properties?
faq.answer: Yardi. Yardi Voyager has dedicated commercial leasing tools and covers office, retail, and industrial portfolios. Entrata supports commercial but its features there are less mature than its multifamily core.

faq.question: Does Yardi publish pricing?
faq.answer: Only for its small-operator products. Yardi Breeze starts at $1 per unit per month and Breeze Premier at $2 per unit per month. Yardi Voyager and Entrata are both quote-based.

faq.question: Can Yardi be installed on-premise?
faq.answer: Yes. Yardi offers cloud, on-premise, and mobile deployment. Entrata is cloud-only.

faq.question: Which is harder to implement, Entrata or Yardi?
faq.answer: Yardi Voyager implementations are known for taking months and requiring significant configuration. Entrata also has a learning curve, but it is delivered as a single cloud platform rather than a set of modules.

comparisons.verdict:
Rent Manager and AppFolio are both cloud property management platforms for professional managers, but they reflect different philosophies. Rent Manager is built for configurability: a full accounting system that runs cash and accrual simultaneously, over 450 built-in reports, an open API, and support for residential, commercial, HOA, self-storage, and mixed portfolios. Its Orion AI adds automation to a mature system. AppFolio is built for speed and consistency: an AI-native platform with agentic automation across leasing, accounting, maintenance, and communications, plus its Realm-X Flows engine for standardizing workflows. It serves residential managers from roughly 50 units to over 14,000.

Rent Manager wins for mixed portfolios and accounting-heavy operations. A manager running apartments, a few commercial buildings, an HOA, and a storage facility can keep them in one system with property-specific handling. The dual cash and accrual ledgers and the reporting library appeal to controllers who want detail, and the open API suits firms that build their own integrations. The trade-offs: pricing requires a consultation, setup can be complex because of the customization options, and the interface can feel dated next to newer competitors.

AppFolio wins on user experience and automation. The unified interface eliminates multiple logins, the AI handles busywork rather than sitting in a separate module, and its Performance Platform methodology gives growing firms a standard operating model. It integrates with Zillow, Apartments.com, DocuSign, Stripe, and QuickBooks. The trade-offs: pricing is quote-based and positioned as premium, the AI-native approach requires training and change management, and the platform is oriented toward residential rather than commercial or association work.

Pick Rent Manager if the portfolio is diverse or the accounting team wants maximum control and reporting. Pick AppFolio if you manage residential units, value a modern interface, and want automation to absorb staff workload. Small landlords with a handful of units should compare both against lighter tools before committing.
comparisons.one_liner: Rent Manager wins on accounting depth and mixed-portfolio flexibility; AppFolio wins on modern user experience and AI automation for residential managers.

faq.question: Does AppFolio support commercial properties?
faq.answer: AppFolio lists commercial among its supported property types, but the platform is built primarily for residential managers. Rent Manager has deeper support for commercial, HOA, and self-storage portfolios.

faq.question: How much does Rent Manager cost compared to AppFolio?
faq.answer: Neither vendor publishes standard pricing on its site. Both are quote-based, so cost depends on unit count and modules, and you will need sales conversations to compare.

faq.question: What is unique about Rent Manager's accounting?
faq.answer: Rent Manager runs cash and accrual accounting simultaneously and ships with over 450 built-in reports, which is unusual among property management platforms.

faq.question: Which is easier to learn, Rent Manager or AppFolio?
faq.answer: AppFolio, generally. Its unified interface is designed for ease of use, while Rent Manager's extensive customization can make setup more complex. AppFolio's AI-native workflows still require training for traditional teams.

comparisons.verdict:
DoorLoop and Buildium are both cloud property management suites that bundle rent collection, tenant screening, leasing, maintenance, and accounting. The difference is focus. DoorLoop is a newer all-in-one product that pitches fast setup and broad property-type coverage, from single-family and multifamily to mixed-use commercial, HOAs, mobile home parks, and student housing. Buildium is a long-established residential platform built for professional property managers and community association managers, serving portfolios from a few doors to more than 15,000 units.

DoorLoop wins on ease of adoption and mixed portfolios. Its Starter plan is listed at $69 per month billed annually, capped at 10 units, with per-unit charges beyond the base. DoorLoop advertises data migration measured in days rather than months. It also supports CAM charges on the Pro tier, which matters if you hold small commercial or mixed-use assets alongside residential. Zapier and an open API are available for connecting other tools. The caveats: the AI assistant, workflows, and QuickBooks sync sit on Pro or higher, and per-unit pricing adds up as a portfolio grows.

Buildium wins on depth for residential and association management. Published pricing starts at $62 per month for Essential, with Growth at $192 and Premium at $400. The platform includes owner reporting, community association tools, Lumina AI for bill scanning and communications, and a marketplace of integrations. The trade-offs are that commercial features are thin, API access is only on Premium, and add-on fees for eSignatures, screening, and inspections vary by tier, so total cost can climb faster than the base price suggests.

Pick DoorLoop if you run a smaller or mixed portfolio, want CAM support, and value quick onboarding. Pick Buildium if you manage third-party residential properties or associations at scale and need mature owner accounting and reporting.
comparisons.one_liner: DoorLoop suits smaller mixed portfolios that want simple setup and AI tooling; Buildium suits residential managers and association firms that need depth and published, predictable pricing.

faq.question: Is DoorLoop cheaper than Buildium?
faq.answer: At the entry level they are close: Buildium's Essential plan starts at $62 per month and DoorLoop's Starter is $69 per month billed annually. DoorLoop's Starter is capped at 10 units and adds per-unit charges, while Buildium's price also scales with portfolio size, so compare quotes at your actual unit count.

faq.question: Does Buildium handle commercial properties?
faq.answer: Buildium lists commercial among its supported property types, but it is built primarily for residential and community association management. DoorLoop includes CAM charges and mixed-use support, which makes it the more natural fit for small commercial holdings.

faq.question: Which one offers API access?
faq.answer: DoorLoop offers an open API and Zapier integration. Buildium's Open API is only available on its Premium tier, which starts at $400 per month.

faq.question: Do DoorLoop and Buildium offer free trials?
faq.answer: Yes. Both DoorLoop and Buildium offer a free trial, and neither has a permanently free tier.

comparisons.verdict:
TenantCloud and TurboTenant both target independent landlords who want to list vacancies, screen tenants, sign leases, and collect rent online without a full property management suite. TurboTenant is built around a free core plan and monetizes through tenant-paid screening fees and an optional Premium subscription. TenantCloud is a tiered subscription product that leans further into bookkeeping, owner reporting, and multi-role mobile apps.

TurboTenant wins for landlords who want to pay nothing to get started. Listing syndication, applications, screening, rent collection, and maintenance tracking are all on the free plan. Premium adds state-specific leases, faster payouts, unlimited eSignatures, and priority support; TurboTenant's site lists it from $149 per year for up to 10 units, billed annually only. The caveats are that Premium is priced by unit band, so costs step up as you add doors, and the product is built for owners rather than managers running third-party portfolios.

TenantCloud wins on accounting and structure. Its current pricing page lists Starter at $18 per month, or $15 billed annually, with unlimited units but a cap of 10 leases; Growth, Pro, and Business raise the lease cap and add lead texting, a lease builder, inspections, and state-specific forms. Separate apps for landlords, tenants, owners, and service providers make it workable for a small manager with a few owner clients. QuickBooks Online sync is a real advantage over TurboTenant for anyone who works with an accountant. The trade-offs are that no free tier appears on the current pricing page and ACH payment fees apply per transaction.

Pick TurboTenant if you self-manage a handful of units and want free core tools. Pick TenantCloud if you need proper books, an owner portal, or QuickBooks sync and are willing to pay a modest monthly fee.
comparisons.one_liner: TurboTenant is the better free starting point for self-managing landlords; TenantCloud suits landlords and small managers who want accounting, owner portals, and QuickBooks sync.

faq.question: Is TenantCloud free?
faq.answer: Not on its current pricing page. TenantCloud lists its Starter plan at $18 per month, or $15 per month billed annually, limited to 10 active leases. TurboTenant is the one with a free core plan.

faq.question: How much does TurboTenant Premium cost?
faq.answer: TurboTenant lists Premium from $149 per year for landlords with 1 to 10 units, with higher annual prices for larger unit bands. Billing is annual only, with no month-to-month option.

faq.question: Which is better for a small property management company?
faq.answer: TenantCloud. It offers an owner portal, a separate owner app, QuickBooks Online sync, and a Business tier with unlimited leases. TurboTenant is designed for owners managing their own rentals.

faq.question: Do TenantCloud and TurboTenant both syndicate listings?
faq.answer: Yes. TurboTenant pushes listings to Zillow, Trulia, HotPads, and Realtor.com, while TenantCloud syndicates to Apartments.com, Realtor.com, and Rentler.

comparisons.verdict:
Archibus and Planon are two of the longest-running integrated workplace management systems (IWMS). Both cover space planning, asset and maintenance management, real estate portfolio tracking, and workplace services for large occupiers. Archibus is now part of Eptura, which folded it into a broader worktech stack alongside iOFFICE and SpaceIQ, and it is delivered as a cloud product. Planon remains an independent European vendor offering both cloud and on-premise deployment, with a strong footprint among universities, corporates, and service providers in EMEA.

Archibus wins for US-based enterprises and public sector bodies. It holds FedRAMP authorization, which matters for federal agencies and contractors, and its Autodesk integration makes it a natural fit for organizations that manage floor plans in AutoCAD or Revit. Eptura's platform adds employee-facing tools such as desk and room booking, Microsoft Teams and Slack hooks, and AI-assisted reservations. The honest caveats: the Eptura rebrand has created some confusion about product naming and roadmaps, pricing is quote-based, and the platform is more than a mid-sized company with simple needs will use.

Planon wins for organizations that want a single configurable system across real estate, facilities, and services, particularly with global or European operations. Its scope includes lease accounting, sustainability and energy tracking, field service management, and smart building integrations, with connectors for SAP, Microsoft 365, and ServiceNow. Analyst firms including Verdantix, Gartner, and IDC have rated it a leader. The trade-offs are enterprise-only pricing, implementations that usually require specialist consultants, and a thinner US presence than Archibus.

Pick Archibus if you are US-centric, need FedRAMP, or live in Autodesk drawings. Pick Planon if you need on-premise deployment, lease accounting, or a global rollout with heavy configuration. Either way, budget for a multi-month implementation and get quotes, because neither vendor publishes pricing.
comparisons.one_liner: Archibus, now under Eptura, fits US enterprises and government with deep CAD-linked space management; Planon fits global occupiers wanting a configurable IWMS with lease accounting and sustainability.

faq.question: Is Archibus still a standalone product?
faq.answer: Archibus is now sold by Eptura, which combined it with iOFFICE and SpaceIQ into one worktech platform. It remains the IWMS suite within that platform for complex real estate and facilities environments.

faq.question: Does Planon offer on-premise deployment?
faq.answer: Yes. Planon is available as cloud or on-premise software, while Archibus under Eptura is delivered as a cloud service.

faq.question: How much do Archibus and Planon cost?
faq.answer: Neither vendor publishes pricing. Both are enterprise products sold on quote, typically with annual contracts and separate implementation fees.

faq.question: Which is better for a US government agency, Archibus or Planon?
faq.answer: Archibus. It holds FedRAMP authorization, which US federal agencies generally require for cloud software, and it has a larger US presence than Planon, which is primarily EMEA-focused.

comparisons.verdict:
Matterport and iGUIDE both turn a physical walkthrough into a 3D virtual tour with floor plans, but they start from different priorities. Matterport is a spatial data platform sold as a subscription, with capture from its own cameras, supported 360 cameras, or a smartphone, and outputs aimed at marketing, facilities documentation, and design coordination. iGUIDE, made by Planitar, pairs its proprietary PLANIX lidar camera with a per-project processing service whose core output is a measured floor plan, with the tour as a companion.

Matterport wins on reach and flexibility. It is the recognized standard for listing tours and integrates with LoopNet, Zillow, Realtor.com, and VTS, so a broker's marketing team can publish without extra steps. The free tier covers one active space, and paid tiers scale by active spaces, with Starter listed from $9.99 per month billed annually on Matterport's plans page. Enterprise plans add SSO, an API, and unlimited spaces for corporate portfolios. The caveats: the best results still call for dedicated camera hardware, hosting fees accumulate across a large portfolio, and models are cloud-dependent.

iGUIDE wins when the deliverable is the floor plan. Captures produce ANSI-compliant plans with a stated 0.5 percent measurement uncertainty, plus room-by-room measurements, and export to DWG, RVT, ESX, and Xactimate formats used by appraisers, insurers, and architects. Pricing is per project, with iGUIDE Instant at $7.99 USD and Standard packages from $48 CAD, with no subscription and no hosting fee, and users own their data. The trade-off is hardware: you either buy the PLANIX camera, listed at $3,499 CAD, or hire an iGUIDE Pro, which makes it a poor fit for occasional users.

Pick Matterport for marketing-led tours, broad camera support, and a portfolio you want to keep online indefinitely. Pick iGUIDE for appraisal, insurance, or construction workflows where measured drawings and one-time project pricing matter more than the tour.
comparisons.one_liner: Matterport is the default for immersive 3D marketing tours across any camera; iGUIDE is the better choice when accurate, exportable floor plans and pay-per-project pricing matter more.

faq.question: Does iGUIDE work with any camera?
faq.answer: No. iGUIDE captures require the PLANIX camera system or a trained iGUIDE Pro operator. Matterport supports its own cameras, selected third-party 360 cameras, and smartphone capture.

faq.question: Is Matterport free?
faq.answer: Matterport has a free plan limited to one active space. Paid plans are priced by the number of active spaces, with Starter listed from $9.99 per month billed annually.

faq.question: Which produces more accurate floor plans, Matterport or iGUIDE?
faq.answer: iGUIDE states a measurement uncertainty of 0.5 percent and exports plans in CAD, Revit, and appraisal formats. Matterport generates schematic floor plans on paid tiers that are suited to marketing rather than appraisal work.

faq.question: Does iGUIDE charge hosting fees?
faq.answer: No. iGUIDE charges per project with no subscription or hosting fees, and users retain ownership of their data. Matterport charges a recurring subscription based on active spaces.

comparisons.verdict:
AirDNA and Mashvisor both sell rental market data to investors, but they answer different questions. AirDNA is a short-term rental intelligence platform built on Airbnb and Vrbo listing data worldwide, with tools for market research, revenue estimation, comp sets, and host benchmarking. Mashvisor is a US-focused investment analytics platform that scores properties for both short-term and long-term rental strategies and layers in a property search, market finder, and data API.

AirDNA wins on depth and coverage for anyone whose business is short-term rentals. Rentalizer produces address-level revenue estimates, Market Insights carries historical and forward-looking occupancy, rate, and revenue data, and the Host tier adds benchmarking and competitor rate calendars. There is a free tier for browsing. Paid plans are listed at $34 per month for Research and $50 per month for Host when billed annually; month-to-month prices are much higher, at $125 and $150. The caveats are that an annual commitment is effectively required for sensible pricing, the Property Manager tier is quote-based, and data thins out in small markets.

Mashvisor wins for investors deciding what to buy and how to operate it. Its analysis shows cap rate, cash-on-cash return, and occupancy for the same property under both rental strategies, and the nationwide property search and heatmaps help narrow markets and neighborhoods. Mashvisor's pricing page lists Lite at $49.99 per month, Standard at $99.99 monthly or $74.99 billed annually, and Professional at $119.99 monthly or $99.99 annually, with API access reserved for an Enterprise plan on quote. The trade-offs are US-only coverage, rental estimates that get less reliable in rural markets, and a monthly entry price above AirDNA's annual rate.

Pick AirDNA if you already run or plan to run short-term rentals and need market-grade STR data. Pick Mashvisor if you are still choosing between STR and long-term rental strategies and want deal-level return analysis on listed properties.
comparisons.one_liner: AirDNA is the deeper short-term rental dataset for hosts and STR investors; Mashvisor is the broader tool for comparing STR and long-term returns before buying.

faq.question: Is AirDNA or Mashvisor cheaper?
faq.answer: AirDNA's Research plan is $34 per month billed annually, or $125 month to month. Mashvisor's Lite plan is $49.99 per month. AirDNA is cheaper on an annual commitment, while Mashvisor's monthly pricing is lower if you do not want to prepay for a year.

faq.question: Does AirDNA cover long-term rentals?
faq.answer: No. AirDNA focuses on short-term and vacation rental data from Airbnb and Vrbo. Mashvisor analyzes both short-term and long-term rental performance for the same property.

faq.question: Does Mashvisor have an API?
faq.answer: Yes. Mashvisor offers a real estate data API, but access is bundled into its Enterprise plan, which is priced on request.

faq.question: Do AirDNA and Mashvisor cover markets outside the US?
faq.answer: AirDNA covers short-term rental listings worldwide. Mashvisor focuses on the United States.

comparisons.verdict:
Stessa and Baselane both replace the spreadsheet for small rental investors, combining bookkeeping, rent collection, and banking in a free app. The difference is where each starts. Stessa, owned by Roofstock, began as an asset-tracking and financial reporting tool and added banking, rent collection, and light property management on top. Baselane began as a banking product for landlords and built bookkeeping and rent collection around the accounts, so its model assumes you will move your rental cash into Baselane.

Stessa wins on reporting and on staying software-first. The free Essentials plan includes unlimited properties, automatic bank feeds from your existing accounts, financial dashboards, tenant screening, and rent collection. Manage at $12 per month billed annually ($15 monthly) adds Schedule E reporting, legal templates, and faster rent payments; Pro at $28 billed annually ($35 monthly) adds unlimited portfolios, advanced reports, unlimited receipt scanning, and up to 3.24 percent APY on cash. Investors can keep their current bank and still get clean books. The limits: property management workflows stay basic, commercial support is thin, and the best features sit on Pro.

Baselane wins on structure for investors running multiple entities. Its Core plan is free and offers unlimited checking and savings accounts through Thread Bank, so each property or LLC can have its own account and debit card, plus rent collection with reminders and late fees, a tax package, and Schedule E reports. ACH rent payments cost $2 unless deposited to a Baselane account, and card payments carry a 3.49 percent fee. The $20 per month Smart plan adds auto-tagging, receipt matching, balance sheets, shared access, and two-day rent deposits. The trade-offs are that leasing, listings, and maintenance are absent, and the value depends on actually banking with Baselane.

Pick Stessa if you want the best free reporting and prefer to keep your existing bank. Pick Baselane if separate accounts per property or entity would simplify your life and you are willing to move deposits.
comparisons.one_liner: Stessa is the stronger free bookkeeping and reporting app for rental investors; Baselane is the better pick if you want property-level bank accounts and rent collection in one place.

faq.question: Is Stessa or Baselane free?
faq.answer: Both have a free plan. Stessa's Essentials plan is free with unlimited properties, and Baselane's Core plan is free with unlimited bank accounts. Stessa's paid Manage and Pro plans run $12 to $35 per month, and Baselane's Smart plan is $20 per month.

faq.question: Do I have to switch banks to use Stessa?
faq.answer: No. Stessa connects to existing bank accounts through automatic feeds, and its own interest-bearing account is optional. Baselane's bookkeeping is built around its own Thread Bank accounts, so most of its value depends on moving deposits there.

faq.question: Which is better for investors with multiple LLCs?
faq.answer: Baselane. It supports unlimited property-specific and entity-specific bank accounts with entity-level transaction tracking. Stessa's Pro plan supports unlimited portfolios for reporting, but Baselane's account-per-entity model is the more direct fit.

faq.question: Do Stessa and Baselane handle maintenance and leasing?
faq.answer: Stessa includes maintenance tracking, tenant screening, and eSigning alongside rent collection. Baselane covers rent collection and tenant screening but has no leasing, listing, or maintenance workflows.

comparisons.one_liner: Zoneomics is the deeper zoning reference with certified letters and the widest code coverage; Plotzy turns zoning into a parcel search with owner contacts, so it wins for sourcing sites rather than confirming one.
comparisons.verdict:
Plotzy and Zoneomics both digitize zoning, but they sell different jobs. Zoneomics is a zoning data company: it aggregates codes from thousands of cities into the largest nationwide zoning dataset, sells reports from $25 and certified zoning letters, offers a free basic search, and exposes the data through an API. Plotzy is a parcel research platform: 150M+ parcels across 3,200+ counties, each carrying a two-level zoning designation, with filters for permitted use, lot size, owner type and sale date, plus owner contact lookup, folders and CSV export. Plotzy publishes flat monthly pricing of $180 or $300 with a 7-day trial.

Zoneomics wins when the question is what exactly this code allows at this address. Its city-level depth, report format and certified letters are what lenders, attorneys and closing checklists expect, and the API suits teams that want zoning inside their own systems. Coverage is the caveat on both sides, and Zoneomics remains the reference point that any parcel platform's sub-level zoning is measured against.

Plotzy wins when zoning is a filter, not the deliverable. Find every parcel zoned for a use inside a corridor or county, screen by lot size and owner type, then pull contacts and export the list; Zoneomics does none of the list building or outreach. For a team running searches daily, a flat subscription is cheaper than per-report spend, while an occasional single-report buyer pays less on Zoneomics. Plotzy is still labeled beta and its sub-level zoning depth varies by municipality.

The rule: source with Plotzy, confirm with Zoneomics. Many land teams keep both, using Plotzy to build the list and a Zoneomics report or letter on the one parcel that goes to contract.

faq.question: Does Plotzy provide certified zoning letters?
faq.answer: No. Plotzy attaches two-level zoning to every parcel and answers code questions through its Zoning AI chat, but certified zoning verification letters remain a Zoneomics product.

faq.question: Which is cheaper, Plotzy or Zoneomics?
faq.answer: For occasional lookups Zoneomics is cheaper: basic search is free and reports start at $25. For daily research Plotzy's flat $180 or $300 a month usually costs less than accumulating per-report fees.

faq.question: Can Plotzy replace Zoneomics for site selection?
faq.answer: For finding and screening parcels by zoning, yes; Plotzy filters 150M+ parcels by permitted use and adds owner contacts and exports. For formal zoning confirmation on a parcel under contract, most teams still order a Zoneomics report or letter.

comparisons.one_liner: LightBox Vision is the enterprise mapping platform with the deeper data ecosystem; Plotzy does the same core job of finding parcels and owners with zoning filters, published pricing and a trial you can start today.
comparisons.verdict:
Plotzy and LightBox Vision, the platform formerly sold as LandVision, both put nationwide parcels, ownership and zoning on a map so you can find sites and the people who own them. LightBox Vision comes from LightBox, a large CRE data company, and ties parcels to its wider datasets through the LightBox ID, with report ordering inside the platform and annual contracts priced on quote. Plotzy is a younger, AI-first platform covering 150M+ parcels across 3,200+ counties with two-level zoning on every record, owner contact lookup, folders and CSV export, priced month to month at $180 or $300 with a 7-day trial and no credit card.

LightBox Vision wins for enterprise teams. If you already buy environmental, valuation or other LightBox products, want multi-seat administration, or need authoritative datasets and in-platform report ordering for due diligence, its breadth and ecosystem are the reason to accept the price and the procurement cycle. Its feature set is deep, and that depth is what large brokerages and lenders pay for.

Plotzy wins on speed and clarity. Pricing is published, there is no annual contract, and a broker or land team can be searching within minutes of starting the trial. Zoning is a first-class filter rather than a layer, so finding parcels by permitted use is a single query, and owner contacts and exports live in the same workflow. The trade-offs are honest: Plotzy is still labeled beta, sub-level zoning depth varies by municipality, and API access and custom integrations sit on the custom Scale plan.

Pick LightBox Vision if you are an enterprise buyer who values the ecosystem more than the price. Pick Plotzy if you are a broker, developer or land team that wants to find parcels and owners this week at a cost you can see.

faq.question: Is LandVision still available?
faq.answer: LandVision is now sold as LightBox Vision. It remains a nationwide parcel mapping and property research platform from LightBox, priced on quote.

faq.question: How much does Plotzy cost compared to LightBox Vision?
faq.answer: Plotzy publishes month-to-month pricing: $180 for Starter and $300 for Production, with a custom Scale plan. LightBox Vision does not publish pricing and is typically sold on annual terms.

faq.question: Which has better zoning data?
faq.answer: Both include zoning. Plotzy attaches a two-level designation to every parcel and adds sub-level zoning filters and a Zoning AI chat; LightBox Vision offers zoning layers and report ordering backed by LightBox datasets. Coverage depth varies by municipality on both.

comparisons.one_liner: Reonomy is the property intelligence choice for existing commercial buildings, with ownership unmasking and debt data; Plotzy is the parcel and zoning choice for land and development sourcing at a lower, published price.
comparisons.verdict:
Plotzy and Reonomy both help CRE professionals find properties and reach owners, but they start from different objects. Reonomy, an Altus Group business, builds connected records for commercial buildings: ownership unmasked through LLCs and trusts, debt and mortgage maturity, transaction history, 200+ search filters and predictive signals for likely sellers, with API and bulk feeds for enterprise. Plotzy starts from the parcel: 150M+ parcels across 3,200+ counties with a two-level zoning designation on each, filters for permitted use, lot size, owner type and sale date, owner contact lookup, folders and CSV export.

Reonomy wins for investment sales and lending work on standing assets. If the play is finding the owner of a specific office or industrial building, spotting loans coming due, or working a market of existing properties with debt signals, its data depth is the product, and the free trial lets you test it on your market. Pricing is not published, and third-party listings put it at several hundred dollars per user per month.

Plotzy wins for land, development sites and zoning-driven search. Reonomy has little to say about what a parcel is zoned for; Plotzy makes that the first filter and follows it with owner contacts and exports for outreach. It is priced month to month at $180 or $300, offers a 7-day trial with no card, and suits solo brokers and small land teams that would not clear Reonomy's price. It has no debt or mortgage data, is thinner on building-level attributes, and is still labeled beta.

Decision rule: buildings and debt, Reonomy; parcels and zoning, Plotzy. Brokerages that do both often run each for its half.

faq.question: Does Plotzy have debt and mortgage data like Reonomy?
faq.answer: No. Plotzy focuses on parcel data, zoning and owner contacts. Debt maturity, mortgage and transaction intelligence on commercial buildings is a Reonomy strength.

faq.question: Which is better for land brokers?
faq.answer: Plotzy, because zoning is a first-class search filter across 150M+ parcels and the workflow ends in owner contacts and an exported list. Reonomy is built around existing commercial buildings.

faq.question: How do the prices compare?
faq.answer: Plotzy publishes $180 and $300 monthly plans with a 7-day free trial and no annual contract. Reonomy does not publish pricing; third-party listings place it at several hundred dollars per user per month, with a free trial available.

comparisons.one_liner: CityBldr is for developers who want buildable units, rents and assemblage math on a site; Plotzy is the broader parcel, zoning and owner search at published prices for brokers and land teams.
comparisons.verdict:
Plotzy and CityBldr both use AI to find development opportunities, and both count land acquisition teams and developers as core users. CityBldr goes deep on the development case: it calculates buildable units for a site, shows market rents by location, finds assemblage opportunities with its Assemblage AI, and includes a CRM for the resulting leads, on quote-based pricing. Plotzy goes wide: 150M+ parcels across 3,200+ counties with two-level zoning on each, filters for permitted use, lot size, owner type and sale date, a Zoning AI chat, owner contact lookup, folders and CSV export, at $180 or $300 a month with a 7-day trial.

CityBldr wins when the buyer is a multifamily or commercial developer whose first question is how many units pencil here. Buildable-unit math, rent context and assemblage detection are real work that Plotzy does not do, and the built-in CRM keeps the pipeline in one place. Coverage varies by market and pricing requires a conversation.

Plotzy wins when the job is broader than one development thesis: a land broker covering a county, an industrial buyer screening parcels by zoning, a retail team hunting corner sites, or anyone who needs owner contacts and an export more than a pro forma. Published month-to-month pricing and a no-card trial matter to smaller teams. Plotzy is still labeled beta, has no buildable-unit or rent modeling, and its sub-level zoning depth varies by municipality.

Pick CityBldr for development feasibility on candidate sites. Pick Plotzy to find the candidates and their owners in the first place; some teams use Plotzy to source and CityBldr to underwrite.

faq.question: Does Plotzy calculate buildable units?
faq.answer: No. Plotzy gives you parcel attributes and two-level zoning so you can screen sites; buildable-unit and rent calculations are CityBldr features, and feasibility tools such as TestFit go further.

faq.question: Which is better for brokers rather than developers?
faq.answer: Plotzy. Its owner contact lookup, folders and CSV export are built for prospecting, and its pricing is published. CityBldr is optimized for developers underwriting sites.

faq.question: Do both offer a free trial?
faq.answer: Plotzy offers a 7-day free trial on its Production plan with no credit card. CityBldr pricing and trials are handled through its sales team.

comparisons.one_liner: Regrid is the parcel dataset you pipe into your own GIS and applications; Plotzy is the finished research application on top of nationwide parcels, with zoning filters and owner contacts, for teams without a data engineer.
comparisons.verdict:
Plotzy and Regrid both rest on nationwide parcel data, and that is where the similarity ends. Regrid sells standardized parcel data covering 100% of US parcels, with optional building footprints, standardized zoning and daily ownership updates, delivered by API, tiles, feature services or bulk files on quote-based pricing. It is a data product; the value shows up when it lands inside your own tools. Plotzy is an application: 150M+ parcels across 3,200+ counties, updated bi-weekly, with a two-level zoning designation on every parcel, filters for permitted use, lot size, owner type and sale date, a Zoning AI chat, owner contact lookup, folders and CSV export, at $180 or $300 a month.

Regrid wins when you have GIS analysts or engineers and a stack to feed. A proptech product, a lender's underwriting system or a national retailer's internal site-selection model wants complete, standardized parcels with daily ownership refresh, and Regrid's delivery options fit that. It is the wrong purchase for a broker who wants answers on a screen.

Plotzy wins for everyone who needs research, not raw data. There is nothing to integrate, zoning is already attached and searchable, owner contact lookup turns parcels into prospects, and the 7-day trial with no card means a solo broker or land team is productive the same day. Plotzy is not a data feed; API access sits on the custom Scale plan, the product is still labeled beta, and sub-level zoning depth varies by municipality.

Decision rule: if the buyer is a data team, Regrid. If the buyer is a person who needs to find parcels and call owners this week, Plotzy.

faq.question: Can I get Plotzy data through an API?
faq.answer: API access and custom integrations are available on Plotzy's custom Scale plan. For bulk parcel data delivered by API, tiles or files, Regrid is the purpose-built option.

faq.question: Which has better parcel coverage?
faq.answer: Regrid states coverage of 100% of US parcels with daily ownership updates. Plotzy covers 150M+ parcels across 3,200+ counties, updated bi-weekly, and adds two-level zoning and owner contact lookup on top.

faq.question: Which is cheaper?
faq.answer: Plotzy publishes month-to-month pricing from $180. Regrid pricing is quote-based and depends on coverage, enrichments and delivery method, and it usually requires engineering time to use.
